10042-the-child-under-eight:
E. R. Murray and Henrietta Brown Smith wrote The Child Under Eight for the Modern Educator's Library, edited by Professor A. A. Cock. Murray, of Maria Grey Training College, covers the child in nursery and kindergarten, while Brown Smith, of Goldsmiths' College, adds her part.

Chapters treat learning born of play, the world as the child's oyster, joy in making, stories, grassy places, rhythm, and the passage from fancy to fact, with a way to God. The book quotes the wonder that an infant is heir of the whole world. Teachers and parents get a humane guide to early childhood.
10459-the-celtic-twilight:
W. B. Yeats published this book of Irish folklore and vision, gathering what he heard and saw among peasants, with little added invention. Yeats says he wished to create a small world from the beautiful, pleasant, and significant things of a marred world, and to show Ireland's face to his own people. His tone is poetic, candid, and mystical.

The Hosting of the Sidhe opens the book, with fairies riding from Knocknarea and calling mortals away from dreams and deeds. Later pieces treat ghosts, saints, and country seers. Readers get a landmark of the Irish revival, where folklore, poetry, and national feeling meet.
10684-a-history-of-freedom-of-thought:
J. B. Bury, Regius Professor of Modern History at Cambridge, wrote A History of Freedom of Thought in 1913 for the Home University Library. The short book traces reason from freedom in Greece and Rome, through its imprisonment in the Middle Ages, toward deliverance in the Renaissance and Reformation. Later chapters cover toleration and the growth of rationalism.

Bury follows the struggle through the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries, showing how free inquiry widened step by step. His style is concise and lucid, made for general readers. The book remains a clear introduction to how the modern mind won room to think.
11043-midnight:
Octavus Roy Cohen wrote this 1921 detective novel, opening on a December midnight in a frozen city. Taxicab driver Spike Walters skids on Atlantic Avenue, parks by Union Station, and watches a deserted street where only the White Star restaurant glows. Cold, sleet, and ice set the mood for a mystery involving a suitcase, a woman in a taxi, and a man named Carroll.

Chapters follow Carroll's moves, a valet's talk, ice cream soda, a challenge, no alibi, and a confession, as clues gather around Roland Warren, Evelyn Rogers, and Hazel Gresham. Cohen mixes hardboiled detail with humour, including Carroll playing piano at a party while thinking of a suspect. The novel gives readers a brisk, atmospheric mystery from the early detective era.
1123-twelfth-night:
Viola is wrecked on the coast of Illyria and believes her twin brother drowned. She dresses as a boy and serves Duke Orsino, who loves the Countess Olivia, who in turn falls for Viola's disguise. William Shakespeare's comedy tangles the triangle until Sebastian, the living twin, arrives to set all straight.

Malvolio the steward, tricked by a forged letter into yellow stockings and smiles, gives the play its cruelest laugh, while Sir Toby and Maria run the plot. The comedy ends in marriages and one man's bitter exit. It stands among Shakespeare's most perfect, funny, and tender plays.
12100-between-the-dark-and-the-daylight:
W. D. Howells published these seven short romances in 1907, late in a long career as novelist and editor. Howells, a leading American realist, here turns to uncanny and psychological subjects, though he keeps his plain, observant style.

Stories follow a man who forgets a whole episode of his life, a widow haunted by a double, a memory that works overtime, and lovers whose pasts will not stay past. Settings run from San Remo to American summer hotels. The supernatural stays ambiguous: ghosts may be real, or may be nerves, guilt, and suggestion. The book shows a realist testing how far ordinary minds bend under grief, love, and fear, without giving up on common sense.
1238-the-city-of-dreadful-night:
James Thomson, a Victorian poet of bleak vision, writes a long poem about a night walk through London, where the streets, the river, and the sleepless wanderers all speak of despair. The city becomes a tomb for hope, and the poem's refrain tolls like a bell.

Thomson, writing as "B.V.," offers no comfort and no dawn: his night is final, and his verse is grave and musical. The poem shocked and moved its age, and it gave pessimism its classic English form. It draws readers who like dark, powerful poetry without easy answers.
12476-ships-that-pass-in-the-night:
Beatrice Harraden's Ships That Pass in the Night, in two parts, follows newcomers, a disagreeable man, Bernardine and Mrs. Reffold through a Swiss health resort and its temple of knowledge. Chapters promise a traveller, a domestic scene, caretakers, a betrothal, a love-letter, the dusting of books, Bernardine's book and the building of a bridge.

The disagreeable man is seen in a new light, makes a loan, gives up his freedom, and learns sacrifice, while Bernardine preaches, writes and grows. Harraden writes a gentle, moral romance about brief encounters that change lives. The title image, ships speaking each other in passing, gives the book its tender theme: strangers meeting, helping and parting.
12671-an-easter-disciple-the-chronicle-o:
Arthur Benton Sanford's 1922 religious tale follows Quintus, a Roman knight who comes to Jerusalem asking what lies beyond death. He weighs the answers of Egypt, Persia, India, Greece, and Rome, and then hears the teaching of Christ in Solomon's Porch. The old question of Cicero or Christ frames his search.

Later chapters stage his vision of the risen Christ and his witness back in Rome, where faith must face imperial power. Sanford writes in a reverent, storybook style, using Quintus as a stand-in for any seeker. The book aims to lead readers from doubt about eternal life to trust in the Christian promise.
12904-light:
Henri Barbusse wrote Light in 1919, translated by Fitzwater Wray, as a novel of war, work, and awakening. A clerk closes his desk at seven, crosses the boiler-house, and joins the hurrying crowd. Chapters are titled Myself, Ourselves, Evening and Dawn, Marie, Day by Day, and The Storm. The book moves from factory routine to the front and to a new vision.

A march scene shows the war's gloom. Four marches pass under a lightless sky, with a halt on a chilly hill, houses green in running water, and orders sending men forward then back through alleys. Barbusse's prose is stark and lyrical by turns. The novel stands beside Under Fire as a major war book.
13141-the-princess-priscilla-s-fortnight:
Elizabeth von Arnim's 1905 novel, signed by the author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden, follows Princess Priscilla of Lothen-Kunitz for a fortnight. Priscilla flees her grand ducal life and hides in the English village of Symford, where a German newcomer is a rare sight. Her uncle once passed through Symford and meant to spend his old age there.

The comedy turns on disguise, money, and the fear of pursuit: her companion Fritzing, no born plotter, mops his brow as a servant demands wages he does not have. Villagers, a vicar, and a boy with quick ears test Priscilla's cover at every turn. The novel is light, witty, and kind, a fairy tale of rank set down among teacups and parish talk.
13157-is-ulster-right:
Published in London by John Murray in 1913, Is Ulster Right, by an Irishman, states the case for Ulster against Home Rule. Chapters run from the Ulster Covenant and Ireland under Celts and Danes through Tudors, penal laws, rebellion, Union, and land purchase. The author argues from history, politics, and finance, not from sentiment alone.

He notes that the Irish Parliament, under Poyning's Act, could pass or reject bills but not amend them, since bills needed approval from both councils first. On land, he counts 73,858 tenants made owners under early acts, and 253,625 under the Wyndham Act of 1903, more than half of Ireland's tenants. The book is a clear Unionist brief on the eve of the Home Rule crisis.
13275-the-gibson-upright:
Booth Tarkington and Harry Leon Wilson's 1919 Gibson Upright, a play staged by Stuart Walker, is set in Andrew Gibson's piano factory office, where he makes the Gibson upright. The cast lists Gibson, Nora Gorodna the piano tester and socialist organizer, Mifflin the socialist journalist, and workers Carter, Frankel, Shomberg, Simpson, Salvatore, and Riley. The play is a comedy of labor and capital.

Riley demands that truck drivers face no more discontent than anyone else, warning Gibson that without trucks his freight cannot move. Later, Carter and Frankel argue over profits, Frankel claiming a right to twenty-six profits when he furnishes the labor for twenty-six. The play treats strikes, socialism, and factory life with humor and sympathy for both sides.
13472-waysiders-stories-of-connacht:
Seumas O'Kelly gathers stories of Connacht in Waysiders, published in 1918. Festus Clasby's shop, with its name in white letters on black, jumps from a rural setting like a commercial oasis, proclaiming the clash of two civilisations against hills pitched like an amphitheatre.

The Can with the Diamond Notch, Both Sides of the Pond, The White Goat, The Sick Call, The Shoemaker, and The Rector follow country people through storms, deaths, and home-comings. A white goat dies before a stable door while mare and foal fear to move. The name of Donagh Ford is praised as an inheritance reaching toward an Ireland risen by her own will. O'Kelly writes western Ireland with pity and pride.
13766-cobwebs-of-thought:
An author writing as Arachne published these short essays on mind, art, and self-knowledge in London. Chapters ask why people know themselves so poorly and why contrasts shape judgment. One essay reads Maeterlinck on Hamlet, while another studies impressions of George Sand. A motto on the nature of thought opens the book.

The writer moves freely between philosophy, literature, and daily life. Ancient views of the soul sit beside modern doubts about purpose and habit. Mistakes, the essays argue, often teach more than success, once a person sees them clearly. The style is reflective rather than systematic. Readers who enjoy Montaigne-like musings will find much to pause over here.
14005-the-ladies-delight:
Printed in London in 1732 for W. James in the Strand, The Ladies Delight gathers satirical poems and prose around the Arbor Vitae, or Tree of Life. An address to well-provided Hibernians opens the pamphlet. Poems trace the tree's root and its spread of leaves over Christendom, claiming use to students of polite literature. A natural history in prose follows.

Ridotto al' Fresco describes the tree's growth in Spring Gardens at Vaux-Hall, under a botanist's care. The satire uses botanical language for bawdy jokes about love and society. Its motto, res est severa voluptas, hints at serious pleasure. The pamphlet suits students of Augustan satire. Its humour is coarse and of its age.
14355-54-40-or-fight:
Emerson Hough wrote this 1909 novel of the Oregon boundary fight, and gave it to President Theodore Roosevelt. Its title shouts the American claim to land up to latitude fifty-four forty. The hero moves among map makers, envoys, and spies in a tense border quarrel. Baroness Helena and other women shape the intrigue. Hough tells the tale in the first person, with dash and a love of bold talk.

The hero follows a veiled lady through dark streets, curious at her flight. When her skirt snags and she falls, he lifts his hat and begs her not to fear. Later he pledges his secret to a woman who says she never knew a friend. She teases him for his odd hours and his dress of hides and beads. The novel mixes border politics with romance, and keeps its hero torn between duty and love.
14394-the-street-called-straight:
Basil King's 1912 novel takes its title from a New England saying about the road to the House Beautiful. Davenant, an Englishman of good family, returns to the company of a woman he once loved, now married and living in Boston society.

Old wounds, money troubles, and questions of honor complicate their renewed friendship, while Davenant weighs the pull of English estates against American plainness. King writes with quiet moral seriousness about wealth, ancestry, and right conduct. The novel is a thoughtful society tale, less sensational than his earlier romances, and more concerned with conscience.
14574-gunsight-pass-how-oil-came-to-the-:
William MacLeod Raine's 1921 western, Gunsight Pass, tells how oil came to the cattle country and brought a new West. Raine dedicated it to James H. Langley, who had lived many of its pages.

Dave Sanders rides, races, and puzzles through cattle trains, Denver, hold-ups, and a gusher. Bob Hart and other D Bar Lazy R boys meet an angel, and a little mother frees her mind. The novel moves from horseback to oil derricks with energy. It is a lively tale of a West changing under its riders' feet, from range to rig.
14756-the-man-in-the-twilight:
Ridgwell Cullum's 1922 novel opens on a crisis, a man with the mail, a figure named Idepski and a yellow streak, before Nancy McDonald and Nathaniel Hellbeam enter the story. Bull Sternford, Father Adam and a lonely figure follow, as conditions are learned and a net is drawn.

The action moves to Quebec, to the open sea and to drawn swords, with the steamer Skandinavia and an affair of outposts in between. Cullum, known for northern and western tales, writes in his usual bold style: strong men, stark country and a woman whose progress matters as much as any fight. The twilight of the title is moral as well as northern, a border between day and dark.
15019-a-queens-delight:
First printed in London in 1671, this household manual teaches the arts of preserving, candying, and distilling as practiced in a fine seventeenth-century kitchen. Recipes run in plain, direct steps: weigh the fruit, add sugar, scald or boil, and seal the result in glass. Perfumes and scented waters get their own section.

Plums, grapes, quinces, raspberries, and pippins each receive careful treatment, with notes on ripeness, peeling, and keeping. The book also shows how much skill ordinary housekeeping once demanded. Cooks and historians alike can use it to taste, in words at least, the sweet stores of Restoration England.
15084-recent-developments-in-european-th:
F. S. Marvin wrote The Living Past. He arranges and edits Recent Developments in European Thought, in the Unity Series from Oxford University Press in 1920. Its Shelley epigraph speaks of hope creating from its own wreck the thing it contemplates. A general survey opens, followed by philosophy, religion, poetry and history.

Political theory, economic development, atomic theories, biology since Darwin, art and a generation of music follow, with a modern renaissance as close. Marvin's contributors trace a generation of change across disciplines, from atoms to poems. The volume suits readers who want Europe's intellectual life after the war surveyed in one place, by writers who lived through it.
1526-twelfth-night:
Twelfth Night, or What You Will, opens with Viola washed ashore in Illyria, where she serves Duke Orsino disguised as Cesario. Orsino loves Olivia, Olivia loves Cesario, and Viola loves Orsino, until Sebastian, Viola's twin, arrives to untangle the knot and marry Olivia himself.

Malvolio's gulling by Maria, Sir Toby, and Sir Andrew provides the comic counterplot, with yellow stockings and a dark room as its props. Music runs through the play from its first line. This text gives Shakespeare's festive comedy in full, tender and mischievous by turns. The songs and jokes still delight modern audiences.
1527-twelfth-night:
Shipwrecked on the coast of Illyria, Viola disguises herself as a page, Cesario, and serves Duke Orsino, who loves the mourning Countess Olivia. Olivia falls for Cesario, Viola loves Orsino, and the triangle tangles further when Viola's twin brother Sebastian, thought drowned, walks ashore.

Around them, Olivia's household stages a cruel trick on the steward Malvolio, whose yellow stockings and cross garters make him a laughing stock. Music, cakes, and ale soften the comedy's edge. Twelfth Night is Shakespeare's most musical comedy, tender, funny, and a touch melancholy. The songs and jokes still delight modern audiences.
16095-the-northern-light:
Translated by Mrs. D. M. Lowrey in 1891 from the German of E. Werner, The Northern Light is a romance of courts, manors, and factories. It opens on a grey autumn morning at a manor by the forest, where two men watch birds fly south and talk earnestly. One is a tall, blonde soldier, firm and erect, whose bearing marks him as much as his uniform.

Later pages bring the cold, statuesque beauty called the northern light at court, praised by all beholders. Her husband's letters come from North Germany. They concern the Stahlberg works and his role as guardian. Duty, rank, and love tangle around her. Readers of Victorian translated romance will enjoy its German setting and its stately heroine.
1686-the-secret-of-the-night:
Gaston Leroux sends his young reporter Joseph Rouletabille to Russia, where General Trebassof lives under daily threat from revolutionaries and his household watches every visitor. The general's stepdaughter Natacha, his wife Matrena, and the police chief Koupriane all circle a plot built on bombs, secret meetings, and coded warnings.

Rouletabille must work out who inside the house can be trusted while attacks keep coming in the night. The novel mixes detective reasoning with the fear of political murder in late imperial Russia. Its tension comes less from one locked room than from a home where danger may already be sitting at the table.
17296-pictures-in-colour-of-the-isle-of-:
This Jarrold picture book offers fifty colored pictures of the Isle of Wight, with short notes, reproduced from photographs true to nature. Its foreword praises cliffs and bays for coast lovers, mills and cottages for sylvan fans, and the Landslip and Undercliff for romance. Geologists find many rock layers close together, and botanists find wild flowers and ferns in great variety.

The book suits travelers who have never seen the island, and those who know it and want a keepsake. Pictures lead, notes follow, and the whole makes a gentle holiday souvenir. Isle of Wight fans will enjoy a handsome, old-style color tour of an island long loved by poets and artists.
18040-thirty-years-in-hell-or-from-darkn:
Bernard Fresenborg, an ex-priest, wrote Thirty Years in Hell in 1904, printed in St. Louis by the North-American Book House. Fresenborg claims he spent thirty years in the Catholic priesthood, then left it to denounce Rome with the torch of Protestant wisdom.

Chapters name who he is and why, then attack what he calls the abominations of Catholicism, and warn Protestant parents about its reach. The book's own title page vows each page is a stinging rebuke to Rome. It is a fierce, one-sided anti-Catholic tract, best read as a relic of early 1900s religious strife, not as fair fact.
18587-the-chums-of-scranton-high-or-hugh:
Donald Ferguson published this school story at Cleveland in 1919. Its hero, Hugh Morgan of Scranton High, faces an uphill fight to build a baseball nine worthy of the Three-Town League. Scranton has just replaced Lawrence in the league, and rivals Allandale and Belleville loom large. Chapters follow practice, a fence with a history, a tragic affair on the road, and a rescue at Hobson's mill pond.

Hugh shoulders a heavy task, wins chums over, and reaches his goal by the final chapters. Ferguson writes in a breezy, boyish style full of diamond talk. The book is a classic school and sports tale of its era.
18803-fighting-for-the-right:
Oliver Optic's Civil War sea story, copyrighted in 1892, belongs to his Blue and the Gray Afloat series, following Stand by the Union. It opens at Bonnydale on the Hudson, where Lieutenant Christy Passford recovers from wounds taken aboard the gunboat Bronx in action with a Confederate fort in Louisiana.

Christy, ready for duty again, leaves his father's house for new service. Chapters follow the Chateaugay, the boarding of the Ionian, a Frenchman in Bermuda, an affray in Nassau, and a question of neutrality. Landings at New Providence, a visit to Tampa Bay, and the surrender of the Reindeer carry the cruise on. The novel gives young readers brisk naval action with a hero back on his feet.
19065-swimming-scientifically-taught:
Frank Eugen Dalton, who taught swimming by his own method, wrote this practical manual for young and old. He argues that fear of water, not lack of strength, holds most learners back. His system starts on land and in shallow water before any real swim is tried.

Dalton gives the breast stroke and back stroke step by step, then floating, diving, life saving, cramps, and water polo. He tells nervous pupils to keep eyes and mouth open under water until dread fades. Readers get a clear, patient guide meant to turn a timid beginner into a safe, steady swimmer.
1908-her-prairie-knight:
B. M. Sinclair, also known as B. M. Bower, tells of Beatrice, a young woman stranded on the prairie who is rescued by a handsome cowboy. She must learn a new language — the language of ranch work, round-ups, and cowboys. A tilt with Sir Redmond, a wild ride, and a search for Dorman carry the plot.

Beatrice asks Sir Redmond what he thinks of a round-up, and he calls it deuced nasty, all dust and noise, while she insists the workmen like it. The novel is a light western romance, with the prairie as both setting and teacher, and it shows Bower's gift for making ranch life comic, brisk, and fond.
19410-critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-e:
John Morley wrote this long critical essay on France in the eighteenth century, first published in London in the early nineteen hundreds. It takes as its main subject the French historian Hippolyte Taine and his account of the years before the Revolution. Morley tests Taine's claims against the facts of French social life.

The essay moves from Taine's view of history to the court, the nobility, and the writers whose ideas spread so fast in France. Morley argues that Taine misses why those ideas took hold there while they faded in England. It remains a sharp guide to how one famous history was read, praised, and challenged by its peers.
19473-now-or-never-or-the-adventures-of-:
William T. Adams, writing as Oliver Optic, wrote this story for young folks about Bobby Bright of Riverdale. Bobby fishes, blushes through sums, buys a little black house on credit, and signs a note he must somehow pay. His travels test his pluck at every stop.

The lessons are plain and practical: keep accounts, face debts, stand up for your rights, and learn from being too smart. Bobby wins his first victories not by luck but by work and honesty. The book was a favorite of boy readers for decades, and its money sense still reads fresh.
19485-the-long-night:
Stanley Weyman wrote this historical romance, published in London in the early nineteen hundreds. A student of theology is drawn into a house on the ramparts and a plot around a secret stone, an elixir of life, and a syndic hungry for its power. A young woman's tale of a small phial sets the danger in motion.

Weyman, known for tales of France, keeps the pace tight: pursuit, disguise, and moral choice in a city under strain. The long night of the title is both a literal night of peril and a test of faith for a hero caught between study and action.
19876-on-the-fringe-of-the-great-fight:
George Gallie Nasmith wrote On the Fringe of the Great Fight about Canadian war service. It preserves the poem In Flanders Fields within its pages. John McCrae's lines speak for the dead of Ypres. The larks still sing above the guns in that poem. The torch passes from failing hands to the living. Nasmith, a bacteriologist, served with Canadian forces in France.

A scientist at war notices water, disease, and sanitation. Nasmith's fringe is the medical and laboratory edge of battle. His memoir balances that work against famous verse. Canadian war writing is rich in such professional views. The book records how expertise served the front. It also helped fix McCrae's poem in national memory.
20395-the-story-of-the-2-4th-oxfordshire:
Captain G. K. Rose wrote the story of the 2/4th Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry and its service in the First World War. The book grew from a series of articles printed in the Oxford Times during the summer of 1919. The newspaper helped the project from the start.

Battalion histories like this one record marches, trenches, and battles as the men lived them. They name the places and honour the soldiers who did not come home. For families in Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire, such a book kept the battalion's war from fading out of memory.
21706-twice-bought:
Gold fever drives this Ballantyne tale, set beside the swift streams that run down from the Rocky Mountains to the Oregon goldfields. Tom Brixton digs hard all day, then gambles away his gains at night in Lantry's store. A big cheat named Gashford wins all Tom owns, down to his last bag of gold nuggets.

Tom's friend Fred Westly argues that honesty is the best policy, but Tom plans to steal his own gold back. Their clash over right and wrong carries the story, with drink, greed, and pride making each choice harder. Ballantyne uses the gold camp to test what a young man will do when fortune seems one throw away.
22430-evolution-in-modern-thought:
Evolution in Modern Thought gathers essays on Darwin's idea and its reach. One passage grants that Darwin did not originate evolution itself. The idea, in rough form, reaches back to Aristotle himself.

Present-day forms descend from somewhat simpler ancestors, the writer argues. Those ancestors descend from yet simpler forms in turn. The chain runs back toward literal Protozoa and Protophyta. About those first forms, he admits, we know nothing at all. Essays like these carried evolution into history, mind, and society. The volume shows educated readers digesting Darwin two generations on. It remains a clear record of an idea remaking every field it touched.
2247-twelfth-night:
Viola, shipwrecked on Illyria's coast and believing her twin brother drowned, disguises herself as a page in Duke Orsino's court. Twelfth Night tangles her service to the duke, who loves Olivia, with Olivia's love for the page, while Malvolio the steward falls victim to a forged letter and yellow stockings. Shakespeare's comedy of love runs on music, mistaken longing, and festive misrule.

Feste the fool comments wryly on them all, and the reunion of the twins unties every knot. The play's songs and speeches give it a melancholy glow beneath the laughter. It stands among Shakespeare's most beloved comedies for good reason.
22619-international-copyright:
International Copyright is a work of argument about authors' rights across borders, treated through ethics and political economy. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. In its century, foreign publishers could often reprint a book without paying its writer, and reformers fought to end the practice by treaty.

The sample lays foundations in economic science, defining it as the ordering of men's relations in labor and in property, the fruit of labor. From that base the writer builds toward copyright as a property question with moral weight. The book belongs to the long campaign that produced modern copyright treaties. Legal historians and publishing scholars will find in it the period's own reasoning, stated in full.
22727-the-land-of-the-long-night:
Paul Du Chaillu wrote The Land of the Long Night, an 1899 travel adventure through winter Scandinavia and Lapland, written for young readers. The catalog record names no author. Du Chaillu, the explorer famous for his African journeys and gorilla tales, here turns north, to the country where winter night lasts for weeks.

The narrative opens on the highroad skirting Sweden's southern coast, then turning north along the Baltic and the Gulf of Bothnia. Reindeer sledges, Sami camps, and the strange light of the polar night fill the journey. Du Chaillu writes with his usual gusto, mixing natural history with personal peril. The book fed the era's appetite for far places, and it still carries the chill and wonder of the Arctic dark.
22997-second-sight:
Lambertson will not talk in Second Sight, a story of unwanted knowledge. The narrator can read him and find out, he reflects, but suspects he is not supposed to know yet. Lambertson did not even mention he was back, though the narrator knew he would catch him five miles down the road. Distance, he notes, makes little difference any more, if he just ignores it.

A gift like that isolates its owner, and the story leans into the loneliness. Knowing what others hide sounds like power until it arrives uninvited. The telling stays low-key and troubled rather than flashy. Readers get a thoughtful piece of speculative fiction about perception, privacy, and the burden of seeing farther than your neighbors can.
23233-posthumous-works-of-the-author-of-:
The Posthumous Works gather writings left behind by the author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Mary Wollstonecraft. In notes quoted here, she judges her own draft honestly. Some incidents, she says, ought to be moved and given stronger shading, and she wished to use criticism before shaping her outline into a story.

Only a few friends saw that manuscript in her lifetime. The volume lets readers meet a major writer mid-revision, weighing how true events should be reordered and heightened for fiction. It is valuable both for the unfinished work itself and for the rare view of her craft.
23482-jacky-dandy-s-delight:
Printed and sold by J. Pitts of London, this early picture book follows little Jacky Dandy, who loves cake and sugar candy. He buys some at the grocer's shop and hops away, pleased, hop, hop, hop, toward the fair and its show.

Mr. Harlequin shows what is to be seen within. There is a lion that never would yield, king of the field, a cruel wolf that prowls the wood and preys on lambs, and a funny, mischievous monkey like a naughty boy. Short rhymes and pictures pair each beast with a moral glance. Small children will enjoy Jacky's hops and the fairground beasts, in a book that keeps its verse plain and its pictures bright.
23703-the-parthenon-by-way-of-papendrech:
F. Hopkinson Smith's The Parthenon by Way of Papendrecht opens at the Ferry Inn at Cookham, where the host bellows for Wilyum at the top of a big-chested voice. The boatman found is a giant, six feet and an inch, straight as an oar. His arms are bronzed by the sun, and his double row of teeth would shame an ear of corn.

He is sick of his job, and shows why: a gentleman whose boat he washed, whose dog he fed, and whose ladies he watched, tipped him a half-penny and shoved off. The coin goes into the river. From this Thames-side grumble Smith's story winds toward art, travel, and the Parthenon of the title, by way of the Dutch town of Papendrecht.
24444-out-like-a-light:
Mark Phillips, the pen name used by Randall Garrett and Laurence Janifer, wrote this science-fiction novel, first serialised in Astounding Science Fiction in 1960. FBI agent Kenneth Malone, who has already tangled with telepathic spies, now faces the case of the Vanishing Delinquents, in which young offenders simply disappear.

Malone's search leads him through a tangle of mind-readers, counterspies, and criminal schemes, with humour and fast-moving action throughout. The novel plays its mind-power premise for both suspense and comedy, as Malone tries to work out who is stealing the delinquents and why. Fans of mid-century pulp science fiction will enjoy its brisk pace and dry wit.
26130-stories-of-the-saints-by-candle-li:
Vera C. Barclay's book frames nine saints' stories in nine days of Cub camp on a green island. Fifteen London Cubs hear a story by candle-light each night: Benedict, Guthlac, Martin, Edmund king and martyr, Francis in two parts, Antony, Patrick, and George.

The Francis tale shows him meeting a leper who could earn nothing and could come near no town. He chooses not to fling a silver piece at a man strangers passed with heads turned away. Francis jumps from his horse to give the coin with a friendly look. Dedicated to two faithful Cubs of the Cardinal's Own pack, the book joins camp life to old lives of faith.
26604-pearls-of-thought:
Maturin M. Ballou compiled this quotation book at Boston in 1881, with Houghton, Mifflin and Company, as a supplement to his larger Treasury of Thought. Ballou dedicates it to his wife, the patient associate of his studies through four decades of happy companionship. His preface describes a lifelong habit of copying and sorting striking passages from known authors.

Entries run alphabetically by topic, from Ability to Fortune and beyond, quoting Cowper, Locke, Bacon, Joubert, Schopenhauer, Montaigne, and Euripides. Ballou compares his use of books to a bee's use of flowers, stealing sweets without injury. Readers get a treasury for reflection and further reading, not a system, with familiar sayings beside rarer finds.
26911-crooked-trails-and-straight:
William MacLeod Raine's 1913 western novel is told in two parts, Curly and Luck, set among ranches, roundups, and small frontier towns. The first part follows a young rustler named Curly as trouble gathers around him, with old scores, a bear trap, and a rehearsed quarrel.

The second part shifts to Luck: a roundup club, an initialed hat, anonymous letters, and a woman who handles a quirt with spirit. Raine keeps the action moving through chases, showdowns, and plain talk, in the style that made his westerns popular with readers of the day.
27193-through-st-dunstan-s-to-light:
Private James H. Rawlinson's Through St. Dunstan's to Light, published at Toronto in 1919, tells how a blinded Canadian soldier found his way back. Rawlinson, of the 58th Battalion, C.E.F., moves from his ticket for Blighty through Blighty itself to St. Dunstan's, the house for blinded servicemen.

Chapters cover Braille, the spirit of St. Dunstan's, air raids, royal visitors, and playtime. In workshops, men repair boots humming ditties, make baskets and mats, practice carpentry, and study poultry-keeping and massage, learning trades by sound and touch on the road from darkness to light.
27246-waiting-for-daylight:
H. M. Tomlinson's Waiting for Daylight, published by Knopf in May 1922, prints twenty-one hundred copies, two thousand for sale, this one number 669. Tomlinson, author of The Sea and the Jungle, Old Junk, and London River, moves from Ypres and a raid night to islands, travel books, and signs of spring.

Later essays take up economics, old sunlight, Ruskin, the reward of virtue, great statesmen, joy, the real thing, literary critics, the South Downs, Kipling, a Devon estuary, and Barbellion. A soldier who went out under fire to hold a wounded German anchors Tomlinson's humane postwar reflections.
27454-in-her-own-right:
John Reed Scott, author of The Last Try and The Princess Dehra, published this novel with A. L. Burt in New York in May 1911, with illustrations in color by Clarence F. Underwood. Its heroine's story turns on a bequest, a stolen treasure, and the question of what a woman can claim and hold in her own right.

Chapters move from Broken and Good-bye through Clarendon, Parmenter's bequest, Miss Carrington, Greenberry Point, and Stolen. They go on to pirate's gold, a symphony in blue, a marabou muff, a lone house by the bay, and the jewels themselves. Scott mixes romance with mystery at a brisk pace. Readers of Edwardian popular fiction will enjoy its twists.
27591-the-birthright:
Joseph Hocking, author of All Men Are Liars, published this Cornish adventure novel with Dodd, Mead in New York in 1897. Its narrator Jasper Pennington tells, chapter by chapter, how the Penningtons lost Pennington and how he tried to get his own.

Jasper is robbed of Elmwater Barton, flogs the Tresidders, and is pilloried for it. He escapes from the whipping-post to Granfer Fraddam's cave, rescues Naomi Penryn from the Tresidders, and falls among smugglers. Cap'n Jack Truscott's gang, his daughter Tamsin, and the wreckers' light follow. An illustration shows Jasper leaping at Sam Liddicoat. The novel is a rousing tale of wrongs righted.
27615-christmas-light:
Ethel Calvert Phillips published this Christmas book with Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1922, with illustrations, and dedicated it to her mother. Its opening poem addresses the Light of the World asleep on Judah's hills, where the night is deep.

Chapters run from Naomi's Garden and One Sabbath through The Trip to Jerusalem and In the Dark, to All the World Comes Visiting. The Shepherds, In a Manger, and The Light of the World close the book. Phillips tells the nativity as a story of light coming into darkness. Young readers get a gentle, reverent Christmas tale.
28117-india-its-life-and-thought:
John P. Jones, a missionary in South India, wrote India: Its Life and Thought in 1908 for readers who wanted a plain survey of the country. Jones covers unrest under British rule, the many faiths of India, the caste system, and the work of missions in places from Madura to Amritsar. The Macmillan Company published it in New York.

Chapters also visit Burma, then part of the British Empire, and describe pagodas, markets, and village life. Jones writes as a Christian observer, respectful of Indian thought but clear about his own faith. The book remains a useful record of how an early twentieth-century missionary saw India.
2827-aslauga-s-knight:
In this Norse-flavored romance by Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué, a knight named Froda collects old songs and legends on the island of Funen. His hall welcomes bards, and his voyages in search of ancient tales frame the story of Aslauga, the hidden daughter of the hero Sigurd. Raised in disguise among peasants, she keeps goats in plain clothes while her long golden hair betrays her royal birth.

Aslauga wins the love of King Ragnar Lodbrok and rises to shine as his queen on the Danish throne. Fouqué tells her rise through song, courtship, and fate rather than battle alone. The tale keeps its interest as a retelling of northern legend in which a concealed past shapes a whole kingdom.
28396-gems-of-german-thought:
William Archer compiled Gems of German Thought, Garden City, 1917, as a wartime anthology of German writing in translation. Archer opens with Thor's hammer-cast, claiming sea and land for Germany, then gathers sections on Deutschland uber alles, German humility, Kultur, the German God, and the chosen people and its mission. Doubleday, Page and Company published the volume.

Archer's introduction frames the extracts as evidence of German thought on war, pride, and destiny. Readers meet the claims in the writers' own words, for judgement, not for praise. The book offers a sharp, contemporary record of how Allied readers saw German ideas in 1917.
28442-ned-bob-and-jerry-on-the-firing-li:
Clarence Young's 1919 boys' adventure, Ned, Bob and Jerry on the Firing Line, sends the three Motor Boys from home to war in France. The story opens with a spy alarm in training camp, then follows the friends through a training camp, the trenches, night patrols, and a sniper's attack.

Bob goes missing, the boys go over the top, and later chapters carry them to St. Mihiel and the Argonne Forest, with captures, escapes, and a black box mystery along the way. Written just after the First World War, the book mixes schoolboy friendship, humour, and battlefield excitement for young readers of its day.
28890-helps-to-latin-translation-at-sigh:
The Reverend Edmund Luce wrote this guide to Latin translation at sight, with an introductory note by the Reverend E. Lyttelton, headmaster of Eton. Luce's book trains schoolboys to read Latin they have never seen before, rather than reciting passages learned by heart. It opens with verses from Virgil's Aeneid and from Rutilius on Rome's mission.

The guide explains roots, word formation, and the habits of Latin word order, with notes on Greek derivations and vowel quantities. Its method suits students who know their grammar but freeze at a fresh page. Readers get a practical Victorian schoolbook, written by a teacher who understood that sight translation is a skill of its own, built by practice and confidence.
29071-chit-chat-nirvana-the-searchlight:
Matt J. Holt published this Kentucky book in Louisville in 1920, in three parts titled Chit-Chat, Nirvana, and The Searchlight. The first part follows John Cornwall, who meets a mountain maid, settles in Harlan, and watches the Saylor family move to the Bluegrass country. Later chapters follow marriages, home life, and travel in Italy.

Holt mixes mountain scenes, family doings, and travel sketches, with later pieces on a conscious mummy, Doctor Brown of Danville, and other Kentucky figures. The book reads as a blend of story and recollection, rooted in the state's mountains and towns. Readers get an early twentieth-century Kentucky miscellany, warm in tone and rich in local color.
29326-the-great-drought:
Captain S. P. Meek published this story in Astounding Stories in May 1932, another episode in Dr. Bird's duel with the scientific wizard Saranoff. The Chief of the Air Corps asks Bird if a maneuver progresses as he wishes. Bird, lowering his binoculars, smiles: the line is splendid. Five thousand feet below, a long line of airplanes stretches north and south.

The general proudly calls it the greatest concentration of air force the country has ever seen. Meek sets Bird's science against Saranoff's schemes, with a drought as the weapon. Readers get a pulp thriller of air power and scientific villainy, where weather itself becomes a tool of war.
29619-the-altar-at-midnight:
C. M. Kornbluth's short tale opens in a bar, where the narrator studies a kid with a rum-blossom nose, broken veins on his cheeks, and funny eyes. The bartender shakes a bottle of ale like a Swiss bell-ringer until it foams in green glass, then tries to push the kid around over scotch and water. The tag line warns that helping mankind may suit mankind, yet prove hard on one person.

Kornbluth builds his story from that bargain: a gift to mankind paid for by one man's midnight altar. The barroom talk turns toward fate, sacrifice, and strange power. Fans of Kornbluth will enjoy a sharp, dark tale where generosity and doom meet at the bar.
29696-the-cruise-of-the-shining-light:
Norman Duncan, author of Doctor Luke of the Labrador and The Way of the Sea, wrote The Cruise of the Shining Light. It was printed in 1907 by Harper and Brothers of New York and London. Its chapters open with Nicholas Top, move to the sign of the anchor and chain, and take a catechism at Twist Tickle. Sinister business, tap-tap on the pavement, and the feet of children follow, with twin islands and a maid of Whisper Cove.

Duncan writes of Labrador folk, sea, and faith, with the warmth and salt air of his best work. The shining light of the title guides a small, brave voyage. Readers of sea stories and Labrador tales will find a tender, atmospheric novel of coast folk and their calling.
29832-second-sight:
Basil Wells sets this short tale in a grim underground future, where men work levels deep below the earth. Duggan, a blind newsdealer on the 10th Level, has lived in his own eternal night. His wife Janith knows to within a few dollars what his stand should make, and he has never saved the thousand dollar deposit he needs. Then a lucky guess in the rockhounds' pool wins him eight thousand dollars.

Pete, an invisible rockhound, hands him the bills, and Duggan pays eight hundred for a ticket on the breakthrough time. The money means he can see again, at least for a while. Wells keeps the tale tight and harsh, with tunnels, levels, and hard bargains. The title points to the sight Duggan buys, and to what it costs him to hold it.
30204-arrows-of-freethought:
G. W. Foote, editor of The Freethinker, republishes a set of his articles from the Secularist, the Liberal, the National Reformer, and The Freethinker of the last five or six years. His preface, dated London, November 15, 1882, says he kept nothing of merely passing interest, and each piece was written with care for more than the moment. Kemp published the London volume, and its opening piece treats religion and progress.

Foote answers critics of his free style by noting that a creed which meets argument with prosecution cannot expect tender treatment in return. He closes the preface with Ruskin's point that bold speech harms less than fear kept too long. The book gives Victorian secularism in its own fighting voice, aimed at clergy, dogma, and the laws that guarded them.
30256-the-heart-of-the-new-thought:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox, associate editor of New Thought, presents the heart of that movement in a London volume from the Psychic Research Company in 1903, its eleventh thousand. The publishers' preface calls the book an interpretation that turns vague, mystic, unreal ideas into a lovable philosophy of simplest construction. Its backbone, they say, is the power of right thought, with tenets startling yet provably true here and now.

Chapters include Let the Past Go, The Sowing of the Seed, Old Clothes, and High Noon. Obstacles, Thought Force, Opulence, and Eternity follow, plus Morning Influences, The Philosophy of Happiness, A Worn Out Creed, Common Sense Literature, Optimism, and Preparation. Wilcox, the preface says, speaks as the voice of the people: practical, clear, and plain. Readers can judge the philosophy on its own plain terms.
3030-the-tavern-knight:
Rafael Sabatini wrote The Tavern Knight as a historical romance of the English Civil War and its aftermath. The contents run from a march and a letter to the sign of the Mitre, Worcester field, companions in misfortune, and the tavern knight's own story. Sir Crispin, Kenneth, Cynthia Ashburn, and Joseph drive a plot of escapes, bargains, counterplots, and wooing.

A boat scene has Crispin commanding Kenneth aboard, taking the oars, and keeping under the bank lest their captors look from a prison window. Crispin declares himself hungry as a wolf and dry as Dives begging for water. Sabatini's swashbuckling pace and Restoration color made the book a popular success, and it still reads as brisk adventure.
30426-rhymes-old-and-new-collected-by-m-:
M. E. S. Wright collects Rhymes Old and New, published in London in 1900 and dedicated to Gladys, Helen, and Jack. Contents group couplets, weather and season rhymes, baby songs, verses on men, women, and children, beasts and birds, alphabets, games, and miscellaneous rhymes.

Opening couplets warn that grass growing in January bodes ill all year, and that a summerlike January calends brings wintry weather until May. Essex rhymes link winter thunder and summer flood to harm for England, while Leicester notes promise plenty of grass but little good hay after a wet Easter. Wright preserves folk wisdom in short, memorable lines.
30447-snow-on-the-headlight:
Cy Warman tells a railroad novel subtitled A Story of the Great Burlington Strike, copyrighted in 1899 with the Roman date MDCCCXCIX on its title page. He opens by noting that good managers rise from messenger boys, brakemen, wipers, and telegraphers, just as admirals rise from naval cadets.

Warman draws on motive-power work and train service to stage a strike that tests loyalty, skill, and command. Engines, yards, and crews carry the action, while managers and men weigh duty against hardship. The novel blends frontier railroad lore with a labor conflict, giving readers both technical color and a human dispute over fair treatment.
30709-god-and-the-world-a-survey-of-thou:
Arthur W. Robinson, warden of Allhallows Barking, writes God and the World, a survey of thought, published in London, Brighton, and New York in 1913, with a prefatory note by Sir Oliver Lodge. It belongs to a Christian Evidence Society series of evidential books.

Contents move from introduction and older orthodoxy to progress of discovery and theological difficulties. Counter-arguments follow in three chapters, then later science and further topics. Robinson surveys modern thought on God, science, and faith, aiming to meet doubt with reasoned, accessible argument for general readers. Chapters on later science weigh new findings against older belief.
30799-the-gno-sis-of-the-light:
Rev. F. Lamplugh, a bachelor of arts of Cambridge, translated this Gnostic text for John M. Watkins in London in 1918. Its full title is The Gnôsis of the Light, a translation of the untitled apocalypse contained in the Codex Brucianus, with introduction and notes. A frontispiece shows the Gnostic cross from that codex, and the contents divide into the translation itself and Lamplugh's notes.

The text opens with praise of a Father of all fathers and a God of all gods, a spiritual mind before all spiritual minds, and a seed of all good things. Its language is mystical and lofty, speaking of heaven brought down to earth and earth lifted to heaven. Readers of early Christian and Gnostic writings will find a short, strange, and striking work, in a careful early twentieth-century translation.
30848-mrs-cliff-s-yacht:
Frank R. Stockton wrote this 1896 novel for Charles Scribner's Sons, with pictures by A. Forestier. Its heroine, Mrs. Cliff, starts alone with her wealth, and the early chapters introduce Willy Croup, Miss Nancy Shott, and Mr. Burke, who takes a growing part in affairs at Planton. Stockton's humor comes from money, manners, and the schemes people hatch around a rich woman.

Later chapters bring a meeting of heirs, the Thorpedyke sisters, money hunger, and at last Mrs. Cliff's yacht itself, with a grove of the Incas, a summer shelter that goes to sea, and a telegram from Captain Horn. The tale moves from a small town to the water, with Stockton's light, ironic touch throughout. Readers who enjoy gentle American comedy will find a pleasant, old-fashioned entertainment.
31086-and-they-thought-we-wouldn-t-fight:
Floyd Gibbons, official correspondent of the Chicago Tribune accredited to the American Expeditionary Forces, wrote this 1918 book as a firsthand record of American soldiers in France. Dedicated to General John J. Pershing and the expeditionary forces, it opens with Pershing's letter of August 1918 thanking Gibbons for his work and noting the Croix de Guerre awarded him by France.

Gibbons writes as a reporter who shared the troops' dangers and wanted Americans at home to grasp what their soldiers were doing and why the fight had to be carried to victory. Brisk, patriotic, and close to the action, the book remains a vivid example of Great War war correspondence turned into history while the guns still fired.
31142-on-the-nature-of-thought:
John Haslam, a doctor late of Pembroke Hall, Cambridge, and author of works on insanity, published this 1835 essay with Longman on thinking and its connection with a clear sentence. Priced at two shillings, the book opens with epigraphs from Hamlet and Goethe's Faust on words, concepts, and the systems men build from mere talk.

Haslam argues that speech, with sounds for every feeling and combinations as intricate as music, is man's most precious gift after writing itself. He adds that reason can scarcely work without language. Short and philosophical, the essay links the act of thinking to the art of saying it plainly, a theme his medical work on the mind made urgent.
3116-literary-copyright:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote Literary Copyright as an address to the first public meeting of the National Institute of Arts and Letters. The institute's original members were chosen by invitation from the American Social Science Association. Acting under a congressional charter, they met at Saratoga Springs on September 4, 1899, voted to organize independently, and adopted a revised constitution. Warner speaks for authors' rights. His argument turns on a paradox.

The author alone among producers is forbidden to sell his product abroad subject only to tariff laws. American law grants a foreign author property only if the book is manufactured into salable form in the United States. Warner asks what folly would forbid importing all foreign manufactures to protect American industry. The address remains a clear statement of the copyright cause.
313-children-of-the-night:
Edwin Arlington Robinson's early poems look at lonely figures with pity and irony. Children of the Night, in the 1905 printing of the 1897 edition, is dedicated to his father and mother. Contents run from the title poem through ballades, villanelles, and portraits.

Richard Cory, Luke Havergal, and The House on the Hill stand among the best-known pieces. Robinson's speakers are clerks, farmers, and failed dreamers, seen with plain diction. The book announced a major American poet. It remains essential Robinson for new readers. Robinson's bleak portraits won praise from Theodore Roosevelt.
32153-songs-of-the-army-of-the-night:
Francis Adams's Songs of the Army of the Night, in a second edition published in London by William Reeves, carries the motto, for the cause of labour all over the earth. Adams dedicates it to Edith. His verses call her his sweet and his child, and recall feet treading side by side through bitter brakes of hell. Its proem, Outside London, opens a sequence that moves through England in three parts.

The contents list In the Camp, Axiom, Drill, and Evening Hymn in the Hovels. They continue with In the Street: Lord Shaftesbury, alongside Liberty, In the Edgware Road, To the Girls of the Unions, Hagar, and Why. Later poems treat Belgravia by Night: Move on, Jesus, and Anarchism. Readers get militant, compassionate verse of the London poor, the unions, and the night army of labour, written in direct, declamatory lines.
32365-a-boy-knight:
Martin J. Scott's novel for boys, copyrighted in 1921, follows fourteen-year-old Frank Mulvy of Regal High in New York. Frank belongs to a parish boys' club at St. Leonard's Church, where Father Boone leads about ninety boys in games, reading, and weekly talks. Early on, Frank gives his packed lunch to a hungry old man on Park Avenue after first passing him by with his friends.

Across seven chapters, from Cross Roads to Knighted, Frank faces tests of honour, loyalty, and courage among schoolmates and club friends. The book frames knightly ideals as everyday choices: telling the truth, standing by a friend, and giving help when it costs something. Its lessons are carried by school, sport, and club life rather than by battles or quests.
32592-let-there-be-light:
Horace B. Fyfe's Let There Be Light, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in November 1952, follows men living after a blitz among cracked highways and ruined cities. Blackie, Sid, Mike, and Vito cut down a tree across a road, hoping the fallen trunk will draw out the machines that still patch the pavement.

The men watch from ambush, whittling and arguing over whether the machines will notice a fresh cut. Fyfe's story turns on human ingenuity against automatic systems, asking what people keep, lose, and rebuild when the old world runs on without them.
32597-accidental-flight:
F. L. Wallace sets this tale among outcasts on the asteroid Handicap Haven, a rock some thirty miles wide. In a society where surgery makes nearly everyone handsome and whole, these men and women bear marks that set them apart, and the rulers will not let them leave.

Docchi, Nona, Jordan, and Anti plead with Dr. Cameron and the Medicouncil for a crew and a ship, and meet a flat refusal. Refusing to wait for leave that may never come, they seize their own chance at flight, taking Cameron with them as they head for the stars.
32704-stepsons-of-light:
Eugene Manlove Rhodes opens this western book by answering Francis Parkman, who once called the westward trek a restless folly. Rhodes replies that the pioneers went west for food and land, and that their work built America. The Great Trek, he says, lasted three hundred years.

From that bold preface the book moves to roundup camps, where a fast cook named Enriquez rules the chuck wagon. Johnny Dines, Lull, and other riders face arrests, jail cells, and old scores. Rhodes mixes tall talk, hard work, and frontier justice in a defense of the pioneer spirit.
32717-wait-for-weight:
Jack McKenty tells of Dr. Allport Brinton, director of a Rocket Research Station that has operated for fourteen years, where every failed test flight ends in a mammoth party. Waking with a hangover to an alarm clock that rings chimes, lights lamps, and starts his bath, Brinton learns that Senator MacNeill is coming to visit.

The staff has nothing to show the senator until a young experimenter, Harrison, produces a mysterious new fuel by accident, and a test rocket's trace stops just short of its mark. Brinton must learn what the substance is, and why it works, before the visit exposes fourteen years of failure. The tale's joke is in its title: success may throw them all out of a job.
32734-fly-by-night:
Arthur Dekker Savage sends Ken and Carol on the first flight around the moon, cheered by crowds on a California desert in 1966. The pair, trained apart since childhood, meet at last in the ship's shadow, while the world watches and moralists protest. Military minds call the flight a crucial experiment that must succeed.

In space the romance turns to danger, for secret orders tell them to abandon ship on landing and enter a bronze portal to caves, using two knives in slotted squares. Ken grasps the grim truth: they were never meant to reach the moon. The tale mixes love, publicity, and a hidden mission.
32822-daughter-of-the-night:
Richard S. Shaver opens with an execution in a garden of live oaks, in a story from Amazing Stories of December 1948. Queen Dionaea's head bounces down the stairway after Druga's sword falls. Her serpent Baena, who lived only through her care, finds the severed head and acts.

Baena bites off his own tail to the tenth joint and presses the stump to Dionaea's bleeding neck, speaking a spell he remembers. The graft takes, and serpent and queen must then share one direction of travel. Druga returns with Eos, whose disk palace and ruby ladder offer a counter to the Goddess Diana's petrifying magic. The tale turns on whether Eos can undo stone and set the garden's captives free.
32885-circle-of-flight:
Richard E. Stockham's short science fiction tale opens on a couple locked in a long, fearful argument as rockets shake the sky above their city. They are, the story soon makes plain, the last two leaders of an opposition movement still alive, and they disagree fiercely about what must be done that night. One urges caution and flight; the other insists on a course that may mean capture or death.

The tale builds its tension from that single clash of wills, set against a city under a regime that hunts its foes. Thorus and Aria, the figures of its framing image, stand for vengeance and healing, and the story asks which of those paths can still win when a cause is nearly lost. It is a compact, tense piece about loyalty, sacrifice, and the price of defiance.
33271-the-riddle-of-the-night:
Thomas W. Hanshew's mystery, copyrighted in 1915, opens with a mysterious affair and a chase that ends in a strange place. Hanshew, author of the Cleek tales, writes of a riddle of the night in which decanters are sampled one by one, a clue that hints at poison, plot, or both. The tale belongs to his International Adventure Library, in a three owls edition made for thrill seekers.

The novel's pace is brisk, its mood dark, and its hero moves through a world of secrets and sudden danger. Readers who enjoy early detective fiction will find a well-turned puzzle, with clues laid fairly and a close that ties them up. For fans of Cleek and his kind, The Riddle of the Night is a lively, old-fashioned mystery.
33677-the-sources-of-religious-insight:
Josiah Royce, professor of the history of philosophy at Harvard, delivered these lectures before Lake Forest College in 1911 on the foundation of the late William Bross. Bross, lieutenant-governor of Illinois from 1866 to 1870, had established a fund in memory of his son Nathaniel, whose income would support lectures in successive decades.

Royce asks where religious insight comes from, examining experience, loyalty, community, and the sources from which faith draws strength. The lectures belong to his mature philosophy, joining American pragmatism (down-to-earth thought) with idealism and a concern for the beloved community (people bound by shared love). Students of American philosophy and theology will find a serious, systematic (step-by-step) treatment, delivered for a general educated audience and still rewarding careful reading.
33826-lippincott-s-horn-ashbaugh-speller:
Ernest Horn and Ernest J. Ashbaugh, both of the State University of Iowa, prepared Lippincott's Horn-Ashbaugh Speller for grades one to eight, copyrighted in 1920. Horn, professor of education and director of the university elementary school, and Ashbaugh, associate professor and chief of the bureau of educational tests, argue that spelling teaching improves in three ways. A better word list, words appropriate to each grade, and economical procedures in learning.

Contents give general directions to teachers and pupils, then directions and word lists for each grade from one through eight, with dictation exercises to close. The speller reflects the measurement movement in American education, grounding word selection in use and testing. Historians of schooling and teachers interested in period methods will find a clear, practical example of early twentieth-century language instruction.
33842-by-earthlight:
Bryce Walton writes a science-fiction thriller in this 1953 story from Science Fiction Stories. The tale opens under a hill in dim light, where a rocket's dun-colored skin rises like a wall. Three trusted workers, men beyond suspicion who worked on the rocket, take Barlow up in an elevator along its curving walls. Scores of men had climbed ladders to platforms and doors for inserting and repairing highly specialized instruments.

In the blockhouse, important political and military figures sit over instruments and charts, waiting and discussing, while Barlow is helped into a pressure suit weighing 700 pounds. Walton builds suspense around a launch, a secret, and the question of how and why a man must die. Readers of cold-war science fiction will enjoy its tense, cinematic opening and its meditation on sacrifice and duty.
33925-the-geological-story-of-the-isle-o:
The Reverend J. Cecil Hughes wrote this 1922 guide to the rocks and past of the Isle of Wight, with fossil pictures by Maud Neal. Chapters move from the rocks and the island's structure through Wealden beds, greensand, chalk, and the Tertiary age, then to the Ice Age, island rivers, and the coming of man.

Hughes explains how the island became an island and how its cliffs hold remains of the Iguanodon and other ancient life. Fossil plates help readers match what they find on shore with names in the text. The book serves walkers and beginners who want the island's deep past in clear, ordered chapters.
34441-the-cry-at-midnight:
The Cry at Midnight is a Penny Parker solve tale by Mildred Wirt, out in nineteen forty seven. A Cupples house of New York brought out the Penny set in cloth form. Penny and her mate Jerry climb Knob Hill on skis in the first part. Night ski light and warm change dread open the tale on that hill. Jerry works as a news man for the Riverview Star sheet in the tale.

Part names run from a no cross sign to a star sapphire end. A storm guest, fade prints, and a glass ball thick the first parts. A cult rite, eleven bowls, and a locked door crowd mid part names. Snatch from flames, a crypt drop, and a dead room close the scheme. Penny takes a task from her news chief in a mid part of the list.
34450-the-nature-of-animal-light:
The Nature of Animal Light is a science monograph on glow in living things. The book stands in the Monographs on Experimental Biology set of works. Jacques Loeb of the Rockefeller Institute edited that set with two colleagues. Morgan of Columbia and Osterhout of Harvard shared the editing work. Greek letters and chemical signs fill the formulae through the text pages.

Fireflies, glow-worms, and deep-sea fish make light with no heat spent. The study asks what that light is and how the body makes it. Notes at the front explain how signs and subscripts stand printed here. Old spellings like atropin stand kept as the author wrote them then. The PH scale name stands in its older printed form as well. Changes were made only where print faults stood plain to the editors. A list of those fixes stands at the end of the book.
35793-seeing-things-at-night:
Heywood Broun wrote Seeing Things at Night, essays printed in New York in 1921 and given to his small son. The fifty-first dragon leads, a tale piece, then how to be a lion tamer and a look at Wells of England. Promises and clocks, drink, and Yale men fill the early set.

Southpaws, buying a farm, holding a baby, turning thirty, Margaret Fuller, and Merrick's women show Broun's range, from sport to stage to nursery. He was the beloved columnist of the New York papers, humane and funny on all of life. Readers get his best short form, warm as talk with a wise friend.
35818-doors-of-the-night:
Doors of the Night is a mystery novel by Frank Packard, printed at New York in 1922. Packard also wrote The Night Operator and the Jimmie Dale adventures. The contents run to twenty-six chapters, from Across the Threshold to The Last Portal. Billy Kane is the hero, first seen pausing in a doorway.

His dark, steady eyes travel over the apartment before he enters. He has dined alone with his employer, as usual. The chapters plunge at once: the crime, into the underworld, and an alias, the Rat. A second-hand dealer, a midnight visitor, and whispering shadows follow. A cipher message, a robbery, and an alibi build the middle. The man with the crutch, mirrored years, and a hole in the wall lead toward the rendezvous and the fight. Packard writes the gentleman-crook tradition at full speed, door after door.
36836-the-men-who-wrought:
The Men Who Wrought is a novel by Ridgwell Cullum, issued at Philadelphia in 1916. Cullum's other tales of the north and the trail are listed after the title page. A front picture shows a man stepping nearer to a steel rail. The contents open with danger, a strange meeting, and a mystery, in that order.

A man named Charles Smith, a lure, and an old mill cove carry the middle chapters. Scenes move to the grey North Sea and to named foreign places. Enemy movements, a chapter called Kamerads, and the crouch of some threat point to a war time plot. The German words and sea settings fit the year of issue, in the thick of the Great War. Cullum wraps that war matter in his usual tale of strong men at work.
36882-a-grammar-of-freethought:
A Grammar of Freethought, by Chapman Cohen, was issued by the Secular Society and published in London in 1921 by the Pioneer Press. Eighteen chapters run from Outgrowing the Gods through What Is Freethought. The nature and utility of religion, and freethought and death, follow. Morality Without God and What Is to Follow Religion close the line. Evolution and Darwinism get chapters of their own.

Cohen's preface leaves readers to judge how far the book lives up to its title. It aims, he says, not at an encyclopedia but at an outline of the freethought position. Freethought is too fluid a term for a set creed. What it names is a definite attitude of mind toward the problems thoughtful men and women face. Cohen writes as a movement lecturer: plain, combative, and sure of his ground.
36904-for-the-right:
Karl Emil Franzos wrote the novel that Julie Sutter put into English for Harper and Brothers in 1888. George MacDonald supplied a preface, saying he offered it freely out of respect for the book. He notes that he had not yet read Sutter's version, but he trusted her past work in the same line.

MacDonald asks how far the tale rests on real life, and he praises its hero warmly. That hero is a Galician peasant with no schooling who lives bravely and stands firm for justice. For MacDonald, good fiction should serve truth and hold up an ideal that real people can credibly follow. The novel then tells how such a man fights for the right.
37966-between-the-dark-and-the-daylight:
Between the Dark and the Daylight stands here in a form whose front pages are house ads for a new book of sleuth tales by Marsh. That book, of a high born sleuth, is shown in its third print. Its price in cloth with a front print is set on the page.

The ads quote the press of the day with warmth. A court sheet says its hand tells a run of sleuth tales in a most sweet way, of the kind of the famed Baker Street man. Their plots are most sly and well worked out, it holds. A Scots sheet calls its hand a skilled pen and backs the book to please all who can be pleased at all.
38604-sir-thomas-urquhart-of-cromartie-k:
Sir Thomas Urquhart of Cromartie, Knight is a life of the Scots writ man of that name, by John Willcock. It was put out in eighteen ninety nine. The front plates show the man him self and his sign in a large form. The book is sworn to a friend whose praise is the prize of the hand. Its list of parts is long and full.

The first part treats the house of Urquhart and its past in that north shire. The birth of the man, his school and high school days, and the coin woes of his home fill it. The great house of his folk, his bent for books, and his trips past the sea come in their turn. The next part calls him home to the wars of the faith pact.
38901-twelfth-night:
Twelfth Night, or What You Will, is a stage fun play in five acts by Shakespeare, in the form made plain for the stage by a famed stage chief of the age. It was put out at London in the age of the wars with France. A list at its front names each part and the hand who played it at a royal house.

That list is a small past of the stage of its day. The duke, the twin pair, the fat knight, and his lean dupe stand in it. The proud steward and the clown, the countess and her maid, fill the rest. The form thus keeps both the great play and the shape one famed house gave it on the boards.
39489-with-beatty-off-jutland-a-romance-:
Percy Westerman wrote this sea romance, published by Blackie in London and Glasgow in 1920. Frank Gillett illustrated the tale of the great sea fight for its publisher. A plate shows Sefton shouting to ask whether a ship can spare any torpedoes, in the heat of the action.

Beatty's battle cruisers met the German fleet off Jutland in 1916 in the fight. Westerman, who wrote shelves of naval tales for boys, rebuilds that day at sea here. Guns, signals, smoke and torpedoes carry young officers through the greatest fleet action of the Great War, told while its memory was still fresh.
40045-voices-in-the-night:
Voices in the Night is a book by Flora Annie Steel, published in London in nineteen hundred. Steel's India novels, including On the Face of the Waters and From the Five Rivers, are listed as its uniform companions. Translation rights were reserved and the edition was barred from import into the United States, its copyright page states. The Berne treaty terms shaped that bar.

Steel wrote chiefly of Anglo Indian life, and her short pieces share that world of officials, soldiers, and Indian voices after dark. The title hints at tales told and heard in the night hours of the Indian station. For readers of her novels, the volume offers the same ground in shorter form.
40119-curiosities-of-light-and-sight:
Shelford Bidwell's Curiosities of Light and Sight was published by Swan Sonnenschein at London in 1899, with fifty illustrations. The chapters began as unconnected lectures at the Royal Institution, the London Institution, the Leeds Philosophical and Literary Society, and Caius House, Battersea. Five chapters treat light and the eye, colour and its perception, the optical defects of the eye, optical illusions, and curiosities of vision.

Bidwell says the subjective phenomena of vision have had too little attention in this country, and offers the field to professional and amateur experimenters. The diagrams run from Abney's colour-patch apparatus and Helmholtz's colour curves to astigmatism charts and multiplied images of lamp filaments. Bidwell writes popular science with a laboratory bench behind it: the wonders are things the reader's own eye does, demonstrated with slits, cards, and spectra.
40904-the-mystery-of-the-pinckney-draugh:
Charles Nott, formerly chief justice of the United States Court of Claims, wrote The Mystery of the Pinckney Draught, published at New York in 1908. The draught in question is a plan of government said to have been laid before the Constitutional Convention by Charles Pinckney. Nott lays out the case like a judge.

Chapters state the claim, follow the draught through the State Department, and test the charge of fraud. Madison appears as witness and as advocate, and his long silence is weighed. Nott also sets the rival Wilson and Randolph draughts beside Pinckney's. The book is a courtroom built around one old paper. It asks how much of the Constitution one man can claim as his own work.
40912-the-pillar-of-light:
The Pillar of Light is a novel by Louis Tracy, published in New York in 1904. Tracy had written The Wings of the Morning before it. A text from Matthew heads the book: the house founded on a rock stood when floods and winds beat on it.

The tale is set at a lighthouse on a reef, with a great bell tolling in fog. Chapters name a signal, a hurricane, and a lottery, plus a man called Pyne and a woman named Enid. A Mrs Vansittart brings fear and change to the rock. Readers get a sea tale of storm, duty, and love at a lonely light.
41280-christianity-and-modern-thought:
Christianity and Modern Thought gathers discourses given in Boston in the winter of 1871 and 1872, printed in 1873. The talks were given at Hollis-Street Church on Sunday evenings and repeated at King's Chapel on Mondays. The American Unitarian Association set the course up to meet a felt need.

The aim, set out in the letter of invitation, was not mere popular talk for the careless. It was to help thoughtful people perplexed by the material and doubting temper of the time. Each speaker worked alone, with no joint plan, in the interest of a free and enlightened faith. Henry Bellows, whose name the catalog gives, was among the voices of that Boston circle.
41764-albrecht:
Arlo Bates, a Boston man of letters, wrote this romance, published in 1890. A German line about falcons flying stands as its motto. Bates opens with a foreword, owning that his tale of a water spirit would not have taken its shape had Undine never been written.

He hopes readers will not set Albrecht down as mere imitation or rivalry of that immortal romance. No effort, he warns, has been made for historical exactness, as the story is a dream of the old German world. A mortal and a spirit meet across the line between their kinds. Readers get a delicate American retelling of the Undine theme.
42188-shadows-in-the-moonlight:
Shadows in the Moonlight is a tale by Robert E. Howard, first set in a famed pulp sheet for weird tales in the mid nineteen thirties. A note at the front tells that a long hunt found no proof the rights in the tale were made new in law. The tale thus stands free for new print.

It opens at a run: hooves crash through tall reeds, a horse falls hard, and a cry of despair rings out. From the dead steed there staggers up its rider, a slim girl in sandals and a belted dress. Her dark hair falls on white skin, and her eyes are those of a trapped beast. She does not look at the reeds that wall the clear space, nor at the blue sea at her back. Her stare is fixed on the horse man who rides in.
42548-the-camp-fire-girls-on-a-yacht:
Margaret Love Sanderson wrote The Camp Fire Girls on a Yacht, printed in Chicago in 1920. Maude Martin Evers drew the front picture, which shows Frances and Jane using their Camp Fire Girl training. An invitation for a cruise opens the fun, as Jane Pellew dances round the veranda waving a letter.

The yacht is called the Boojum, and Sergeant Murphy helps the girls weigh anchor. They stop at the landing of the Pilgrims, explore Gloucester, and reach Hurricane Island. What Frances found, the affairs of Breck, and a tragedy that begins late in the cruise raise the stakes. Camp Fire skills, songs, and pluck carry the girls through a sailing holiday with real risk in it.
42802-the-riddle-of-the-mysterious-light:
Mary E Hanshew and Thomas W Hanshew wrote The Riddle of the Mysterious Light for the Scotland Yard Mystery Library. McKinlay, Stone and Mackenzie issued the book in New York. Copyright dates of nineteen hundred twenty and twenty one appear on the title page. Thirty two chapters carry the case load.

The hero is Hamilton Cleek, a famed solver of hard crimes. He works with Maverick Narkom, the head of Scotland Yard. The first case traps Cleek among Paris gangs. Later chapters take up a haunted village and a church ghost. A safe with a time lock and a stolen statue add more puzzles. Each case ends with Cleek laying out the truth.
43488-connaught:
Stephen Gwynn described Connaught for the Beautiful Ireland travel series. Alexander Williams painted the views that fill the small book. Blackie and Son issued it in London in nineteen hundred twelve. Leinster, Ulster, and Munster stand as its three sister volumes.

Connaught is the best marked of Ireland’s four shires, Gwynn holds. Its ways match the English stage Irishman more than any other’s. Shawled heads and bare feet line the whole Atlantic shore there. Galway and Mayo women wear the red skirt dyed with madder root. Lough Breenbannia fronts the book in a soft west light plate. Killary Bay, Croagh Patrick, and Achill Island fill the view list. Lough Corrib and Lough Mask shine in the mid plates here. Gwynn walks the reader through bog, bay, and old town in turn.
43843-lafayette-we-come-the-story-of-how:
Rupert Holland tells the life of the Marquis de Lafayette in Lafayette, We Come, printed in 1918. George Jacobs of Philadelphia put out the book while a new war ran in France. The tale starts at the castle of Chavaniac in Auvergne, where Lafayette was born on September 6, 1757. Holland shows a rich young lord who gave up ease to sail for America. There he fought as a volunteer and won the trust of George Washington.

Later parts trace his aid to the United States from France and his hope to free France too. Storm, prison, exile, and the days of Napoleon follow in turn. The last part turns to 1918, when United States troops crossed to fight in France. Holland frames that march as a debt paid back to a friend of free rule.
44401-the-phantom-yacht:
The Phantom Yacht is a girls' mystery novel by Carol Norton, published in New York by the Burt Company in 1928. It belongs to a mystery and adventure series for girls of twelve to sixteen. Norton also wrote Bobs, a Girl Detective, and The Seven Sleuths' Club.

Twenty-seven chapters pack the plot. Friends part, ghosts are banished, a lost mother is sought, and a light shows in the dark before the phantom yacht itself appears. A bleached skeleton, sounds in a loft, a gloomy swamp, and an old ruin at midnight follow. Letters of importance and a ransacking keep the pace up.
