A frontispiece line cries that a character has found what he wanted. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
44973-stray-pebbles-from-the-shores-of-t:
Stray Pebbles from the Shores of Thought is a book of poems by Elizabeth Porter Gould. It came out in Boston in 1892. The poems are sorted into clear groups, with a set of sonnets near the end.

One group sings of nature, from summer hours to a butterfly in flight. A second group treats love, loss and longing. Other poems mark birthdays, praise Walt Whitman, and recall friends and kin. A last, lighter group was written for her young nephews and nieces. The verse is warm and direct, and much of it grows out of home life. A short set for young kin shows her lighter, playful side at the close.
45086-birds-in-flight:
W P Pycraft, a zoologist at the British Museum, published Birds in Flight in London in 1922, with drawings by Roland Green. Pycraft starts with the wing itself, its feathers, bones, and muscles, and the air spaces in a bird's body. He then looks back to the first known bird and the long line that led to the birds of today.

From there the book takes up wing shapes and sizes, soaring, hovering, diving, and taking off. It asks how fast birds fly, how high they climb, and what loads they can carry. Chapters also cover flight in flocks, the tail and neck in flight, and tests on wing size. It suits readers who watch birds and want to know how flight works.
45344-artificial-and-natural-flight:
Hiram Maxim's book on flight, issued by Whittaker and Company in London and New York in 1908 with ninety-five illustrations, argues the case for the flying machine. Its front pages carry an advertisement for another aeronautics handbook, but the title page and preface that follow are Maxim's own. He dates his interest to 1856, when he was sixteen and already a fair mechanician.

His father, a thinker and a clever mechanician, had sketched a machine of the helicopter type with two screws on one axis, turning in reverse directions. The plan wanted large screws of very fine pitch and a forward tilt of the axis for horizontal motion. His father saw that no motor light enough yet existed, but foresaw an engine worked by explosions in the cylinder.
45414-a-handbook-of-freethought:
A Handbook of Freethought is a store book of proofs against the church faith, chose by Bell. It came out at New York from a house named for truth seek, in a row of such works. Its full head tells its store: a vast sum of proof in brief, set form.

Its first words tell how it was made. He aimed, he says, to put in tight and trim form a large sum of proof against the myths of the church. He had oft felt the need of such a work for his own use. The stuff is culled from some of the best pens, live and dead. Its run heads, part heads, and classed themes make it a true hand book for the askers and truth seekers of its day.
46556-the-isle-of-wight:
Mitton wrote The Isle of Wight for the Beautiful Britain series, published at London by Black. A frontispiece shows Shanklin Chine, the picturesque ravine carved by a small stream on the town's south side. The contents are short: the island first, then Carisbrooke and its memories.

Concerning literary men and makers of history follows, then yachts and men of war, for Cowes was the yachting capital of the world. The scenery and how it came to be, and footprints of the invaders, close the text. The illustrations list reads like a holiday: Sandown Bay, the Undercliff, Freshwater Bay, Godshill, and the Needles. Geraldine Mitton wrote many of these little island and city guides. The book packs the island into sixty pages of text. It is a souvenir with real information in it.
46777-happiness-as-found-in-forethought-:
Horace Fletcher wrote this self-help book, Happiness as Found in Forethought minus Fearthought, copyrighted in 1898 and here in its fourteenth thousand. Fletcher's other works line the front pages: the A B-Z of our own nutrition and The New Menticulture, the A-B-C of true living. The contents map his system: hypothesis, theory, and prefatory definitions first. Then the analysis of fear and its baleful effects.

How to eliminate fear and cure its special forms follows. Later chapters bear his slogans in their titles: stop importing, the impotence of pain, unhappy unless miserable, and call suspicion a liar. Love cannot be qualified, one insists. Fletcher, famous for teaching America to chew its food to liquid, applied the same optimism to the mind. Fear, renamed fearthought, is the enemy to be chewed away.
4793-the-fiend-s-delight:
Dod Grile published The Fiend's Delight at New York in 1873, dedicating it, with mock reverence, to the immutable and infallible goddess Good Taste. The dedication thanks her for condemning all superior authors, and hopes to propitiate her creators and expounders, signed by her devout worshipper, the author. A preface and a long contents list follow, under the heading Some Fiction.

Stories include One More Unfortunate, The Strong Young Man of Colusa, and The Glad New Year, with Love's Labour Lost and Little Isaac. The Heels of Her, A Tale of Two Feet, and The Scolliver Pig follow, with A Bit of Chivalry and Deathbed Repentance. The New Church that was not Built, A Tale of the Great Quake, Johnny, and The Child's Provider lead to boys who began wrong, a Kansas incident, and Mr. Grile's girl. Readers get sharp, satirical California sketches, witty and deliberately irreverent.
48478-linda-carlton-s-ocean-flight:
Linda Carlton's Ocean Flight is a girls' adventure novel by Edith Lavell, printed by the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron, Ohio. The copyright is 1931. A front picture shows Linda climbing into her plane without the slightest misgiving. The first chapter is called In the Fog. Linda Carlton is a young aviatrix who has been flying her Arrow biplane for three months.

The tale opens at the doctor's office. Doctor Ginsley, the Carlton family physician for years, tells Linda she is in perfect physical condition. Her Aunt Emily wanted her checked before she goes any further with aviation. Linda means to take a thorough course at a good ground school and win a transport license, the highest rank. Linda waits for her father to come home.
48851-a-balloon-ascension-at-midnight:
George Eli Hall wrote of a balloon ascension at midnight, printed at San Francisco in 1902 with silhouettes by Gordon Ross. The author's autograph edition was limited to thirty copies on imperial Japan vellum, fifteen for sale. There is no conquest to which the whole human race aspires more ardently than the empire of the air, Santos Dumont is quoted at the front.

Hall and the daring French aeronaut Etienne Giraud left Paris in the balloon Rolla and landed at Cezy, five kilometers from Joigny, after a crossing of ten hours, Le Figaro reported. We had agreed that I should call for him after dinner, not later than eleven, Hall begins. At the gas works of Saint Denis the little bubble of a balloon raised a touch of alarm. Night air travel gets a bright first hand tale.
50339-the-spider-web-the-romance-of-a-fl:
The Spider Web is the romance of a flying-boat war flight, signed only with the initials P I X. Blackwood printed the book in Edinburgh and London in 1919. The author gives it to the officers and men of the War Flight at Felixstowe.

Thanks are due, the front matter says, to the editors of Blackwood's Magazine and of The Times. Plates show a Porte Baby flying-boat with a Bristol Bullet scout on its top plane. A chart maps the patrol area, with submarines sighted and bombed over four months. The chapters name the spider web patrol, a phantom flight, and the sticky ends of three German boats. The fatal fountain and the end of another boat follow. A last chapter looks ahead to running the United States mail by air.
50735-too-fat-to-fight:
Rex Beach wrote this war comedy, printed by Harper in New York in January 1919. Skidmore drew the pictures. Beach was famed for Alaska tales like The Spoilers and The Iron Trail. His hero here is Norman Dalrymple, known to friends as Dimples.

Dimples is very fat, fond of chairs, and proud to buy a one-way ticket to the Plattsburg training camp. Plates show him bulging out of his uniform, his tiny cap perched like the top of a ripe berry. He gains a pound at camp and orders corn-starch pudding anyway. Chapters take him through a YMCA hut and up Hill Two Eighty-Five. Beach writes the tale as warm farce about a soft man in a hard war.
50935-star-bright:
Star, Bright is a science fiction story by Mark Clifton, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in July 1952. Its narrator watches his three year old daughter, Star, with growing wonder. At three, she should not be able to cut out and paste together a Möbius strip by reasoning.

Star traces the strip's single surface with a crayon, proving she understands it. Then she sits for half an hour, chin in hand, thinking with painful concentration. The children in the story insist there is no past or future; it all just is, and they have reason to know. Clifton builds the tale on gifted children whose minds work outside ordinary time. The father's quiet diary entries turn parental pride slowly into awe and unease.
5140-he-knew-he-was-right:
Anthony Trollope's novel, serialised in 1868 and 1869, studies a marriage destroyed by jealousy. Louis Trevelyan becomes convinced, without proof, that his wife Emily favours Colonel Osborne, and his certainty hardens into obsession, driving the couple apart and drawing family, friends, and lawyers into the wreck.

Trollope builds the tragedy from small misunderstandings that pride will not let go, and the title states the moral: knowing one is right can itself be the fault. The novel stands among his finest psychological studies, and it still reads as a sharp account of how suspicion, once indulged, becomes its own evidence.
51726-wall-of-crystal-eye-of-night:
Algis Budrys wrote this science fiction tale, printed in Galaxy magazine in December 1961. Its epigraph calls the hero a vendor of dreams, purveying worlds beyond imagining to others. Yet his doom is this: he cannot see what he must learn of his own. Rufus Sollenar stands fifty paces from his desk, hands in his hip pockets, watching the night world through the crystal wall over Manhattan.

Below him the city is traced in light; above, stars, and a falling rocket streaks toward the Long Island facility. His hand carries rings of utility jewels, and his secretary's voice moves through the air to his ear. Budrys builds a future of showrooms and dream-sellers with cold, exact style. The tale turns on what its dream merchant cannot picture for himself.
51834-never-come-midnight:
Never Come Midnight, by Christopher Grimm, is a science fiction tale from Galaxy of May 1958. Dillon drew the pictures for the story. A blurb sets its hook in one breathless line.

Across the void came a man who could not have been born, from a world that could never have been conceived. He came to demand his birthright of an Earth that would die to pay it. The tale opens in talk: Jan Shortmire tells Peter Hubbard of a son. Shortmire never married in his hundred and fifty-five years, and Hubbard knows it. In that age, science, law, and custom had made the accident near impossible. Shortmire is glad of an heir to keep the state from his estate. He rages that the state barred him from selling his patents, as Dyall sold his.
51859-bruno-or-lessons-of-fidelity-patie:
Jacob Abbott wrote this children's book as the first of Harper's Story Books, a monthly series begun in December 1854. Bruno is a dog, and the tales about him teach faithfulness, patience, and self-denial. Abbott, a famed writer for the young, meant the series to instruct as well as to please.

The preface explains the plan: stories, dialogues, lives, and tales, all rich with engravings. In the frame story, the boy Hiram learns to forgive by watching Bruno forgive. The book uses a pet's loyalty to make moral lessons stick without long lectures. It is a warm sample of the reading once placed in American children's hands.
52058-isle-of-wight:
A R Hope Moncrieff described the Isle of Wight in words. A Heaton Cooper painted its scenes in color. Adam and Charles Black issued the book at London in 1908. The Needles front the volume as first plate. Ten chapters walk the island round. The Island opens the tour at page one.

Ryde and Newport take the next two chapters. The East Side and the Undercliff follow in turn. The Back of the Island heads chapter six. Freshwater and the Needles fill the seventh. Yarmouth and Cowes come near the end. The Gates of the Island close the book. Twenty-four plates face their pages in the list. Carisbrooke Castle and Osborne House stand pictured there. The Island, its people call it, the text opens. Painted guide books sold the small island's cliffs and chines to rail and steamer tourists.
53337-linda-carlton-s-hollywood-flight:
Linda Carlton Hollywood Flight is a girls aviation story by Edith Lavell, published in 1933. Burt Company issued the book at New York and Chicago in that year. Lavell is named as author of the Girl Scout series and of the earlier Linda Carlton books. A frontispiece shows two girls waiting in breathless suspense at page 113.

 Contents open with A Flash on the Screen and A Dangerous Landing for the heroine. The Cross Country Flight and Hollywood follow in the list of chapters of the book. The Vanishing Double and The Forged Signature carry the mystery into the film world in turn. Lavell girl pilot was one of the heroines of the air minded years after Lindbergh. Her Hollywood flight joins the two glamours of 1933, the aeroplane and the picture studio, in one plot of stunt flying and studio intrigue.
53622-what-nietzsche-taught:
Willard Huntington Wright wrote What Nietzsche Taught, printed in New York in 1915. Its motto is Nietzsche's own: he writes for a race of men not yet in being, the lords of the earth. Wright gives the book to Mencken, the critic who did most to stir American study of Nietzsche.

A full list of the works in English fronts the study, from Human, All-Too-Human to Zarathustra and Beyond Good and Evil. Wright then walks through the thought book by book, in plain order. He later won fame under another name for detective tales. Readers get the clearest early American guide to a hard master.
54-40-or-fight: Emerson Hough sets this novel among map makers, diplomats, and secret agents during a border dispute. Its central figure moves between drawing rooms and secret service work, where a baroness, a second woman, and statesmen shape the plot. The chapters follow argument, intrigue, and a long chase that tests loyalty and nerve. Hough mixes romance and political maneuver into a brisk adventure of maps, messages, and disputed ground.
54292-what-jesus-taught:
Widtsoe wrote this study of the teachings of Jesus for the Deseret Sunday School Union, which published it at Salt Lake City. It is a Latter-day Saint textbook, built lesson by lesson with pictures of Palestine and the life of Christ. Its frontispiece is Hunt's Light of the World.

The first lesson takes Jesus at twelve in the temple, about his Father's business. Later lessons ask what it means to know God, what Jesus said of himself, and who the Holy Ghost is. Napoleon's testimony to Christ opens the argument. Widtsoe writes for Sunday school teachers in plain, earnest prose. The plan is to move from knowledge of God to the duties of his followers, with each chapter headed by its questions and testimonies.
54973-the-brighton-boys-in-transatlantic:
Lieutenant James Driscoll wrote The Brighton Boys in Transatlantic Flight for his Brighton Boys series. The Winston Company of Philadelphia held it under copyright in 1920. Earlier books sent the boys to the flying corps, the trenches, and the battle fleet. Big Jack Carew, named for his size at school, opens this tale.

The boys wait in a chilly shack for the hop-off of a great flight. A stranger arrives, and treachery is afoot: a tamperer is caught at their plane. Orders send them to Washington, then off to Europe with papers for Paris. An enemy plane pursues them through a hurricane, and a battle in the clouds follows. Fuel from a tanker and a ten-mile glide keep them aloft. Their arrival in Paris, the book claims, assures world peace.
55009-the-botanical-lore-of-the-californ:
The Botanical Lore of the California Indians sets down the plant medicine of the author's people. John Bruno Romero wrote the book, and Vantage Press published it at New York in 1954. Romero dedicates the work to his uncle, a chief of the Palm Springs country. Contents promise a book of herbs and a legend of mineral springs.

Each herb entry joins the Indian name to the Latin one. Tea from one plant, the text says, fought the smallpox plague of 1857. Blue eyed grass served for stomach worms, and monkey flower for other ills. Romero gives the look, the place, and the use of each plant. Indexes sort the herbs by name and by ailment. A plea closes the front matter: help save the wild plants for mankind.
55276-twilight:
Twilight is a novel by Frank Danby, the pen name of a British author. The book came out in New York in the year nineteen sixteen. Its first pages list a shelf of past novels by the same hand. The tale is told by a sick man who takes a house to rest.

He signs for a small house in a place called Pineland with no look at it. Three months of nerve pain, held in check by drugs, dull his care. The house agent proves as loose with truth as most of his kind. Sixteen chapters spin out what the move brings to his door in time. Grief and self doubt shade the tone from the first page.
56249-the-problem-of-manflight:
James Means of Boston wrote The Problem of Manflight, a short pamphlet sold for ten cents in 1894. Its cover shows the flight of Otto Lilienthal in Prussia in 1893, drawn from a photograph taken in the moment. Means opens by noting how interest in flight grows as the century nears its close.

Everyone, he says, wants to know what the flying machine of the future will look like. Readers also wonder which century, the nineteenth or the twentieth, will claim the prize. Means surveys the state of the art as it stood before powered flight: gliders, soaring, and the hard facts of lift and control. The pamphlet catches the last years when human flight was still an open problem argued in print.
56730-tony-the-tramp-or-right-is-might:
A boys' novel by Horatio Alger Jr, in a New York Book Company edition of 1909. The volume belongs to a uniform new edition of the Alger stories. Its front matter boasts of Alger's hold on boys. His heroes, it says, are living boys who do things. Pluck, perseverance, and independence form the promised lessons. The frontispiece shows Tony transformed at Middleton Hall.

Tony travels with a sinister, dark-complexioned companion. The man wears a slouch hat over a low, receding brow. Piercing black eyes look out beneath its brim. Strangers take him for gypsy blood, and rightly. Chapter one calls the pair simply two tramps. Tony's road runs from that company toward honesty and a hall. Alger built an industry on such rises from the street.
56823-winnetou-the-apache-knight:
Winnetou, the Apache Knight adapts the German stories of May for boys and girls. Marion Ames Taggart made the adaptation, and Benziger Brothers printed it at New York in 1898. The narrator calls himself Jack Hildreth. The companion volume was The Treasure of Nugget Mountain.

Nineteen chapters tell the western tale. Toward the Setting Sun opens it, then My First Buffalo and Wild Mustangs. A grizzly and a meeting lead to the speech of the Apache chief. A compact with the Kiowas, Sam Hawkins spying, and the capture of Winnetou build the middle. Then come a duel, capture by the Apaches, a trial for life, and a swim for freedom. Tangua's punishment and the end of Rattler follow. Teaching Winnetou and the burial of Kleki-Petrah close the book.
56973-adrift-in-the-city-or-oliver-conra:
Horatio Alger Jr tells a boy's fight in Adrift in the City; or, Oliver Conrad's Plucky Fight, from the John C Winston Company of Philadelphia, copyrighted in 1895. Alger had written the Ragged Dick, Tattered Tom, and Luck and Pluck series. A plate shows Oliver resenting his step-brother's interference, and the contents run to forty chapters.

Two young enemies open it: Roland Kenyon's secret, a dangerous letter, and Oliver's journey follow. Oliver loses his place, becomes an outcast, survives a midnight attack, and meets Mr Denton of Chicago. A startling telegram and a thunderbolt close the tale. Pluck wins its way.
56984-sussex-gorse-the-story-of-a-fight:
Sussex Gorse, the Story of a Fight, is a novel by Sheila Kaye-Smith. Knopf published it in New York in 1916. Eight books divide the long struggle. A prologue called The Challenge opens the tale. Book titles run from Beginning to Victory.

The prologue sets a country fair in October 1835. Boarzell Fair had met yearly beyond memory. The moor lies five miles from Rye. Gorse and heather cover its hummocked crest. Gipsies camp on the fair's flanks. Showmen's caravans line up beside them. Stalls pile sweets, ribbons, and tin lockets. The wealden clay oozes red through the poor soil. From this ground the fight of the title begins.
57577-admiral-s-light:
Henry Milner Rideout's Admiral's Light was published by Houghton, Mifflin at Boston and New York in November 1907. Rideout also wrote Beached Keels and The Siamese Cat. Eleven chapters run from The Gypsy Mare through Captain Florio, The Saffron Man, and Pan's Pipes to Habakkuk's Light, The Other Camp, and The Risk. Martin Justice drew the frontispiece of Anna Hilliard, and Woodbury the half-titles.

The first chapter puts Miles, the lighthouse keeper's boy, on his third inspection of the night. The lamp burns as bright at midnight as at sunrise, and he bids it good-night as Beast before whistling down the path by the river. Seaweed at low tide and Orion's red shoulder-star set the coast mood. Rideout writes a Maine-coast tale of a light station, camps, and young people, with the lamp as its fixed point.
58091-the-honorable-miss-moonlight:
Onoto Watanna, the pen name of Winnifred Eaton, published The Honorable Miss Moonlight with Harper in 1912. Her earlier A Japanese Nightingale had made the name famous. The price list inside puts this volume at a dollar net, post octavo, beside Tama and A Japanese Blossom.

Eaton, born in Montreal to an English father and a Chinese mother, wrote as a Japanese lady for a market eager for Japan. Her novels mix the two trades: romance in Japanese dress, written with a Canadian's knowledge of what western readers wanted. Miss Moonlight belongs to the run of tales that kept her among the best-paid magazine writers of her day, before she turned to screenwriting and western ranch life.
58204-a-history-of-greek-economic-though:
A History of Greek Economic Thought is a study by Trever. He set it as his proof work for the high degree at a great school of Chicago. It came out from that schools press in the mid war years. Its rights were held that year, with all rights kept. A note at its front tells how its print form was set.

Slant text stands by marks in that form. Notes are moved to the ends of their parts. Its theme is the lore of wealth in the old Greek world. It tells how its sages thought on trade, coin, and price. It tells how they thought on farm work, and on the dues of the rich and the poor. It stands as a young fields map of its past.
59329-birthright:
Birthright is a science fiction story by April Smith, printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in August 1955. The magazine text is the source of this edition.

Cyril Kirk, the highest man in his class, has been posted to Nemar, a planet nobody can explain to him. He rides the spaceship in a fury while the other passengers whisper about the gold badge of a Planetary Administrator on his uniform. They guess this is his first appointment and cannot guess why a man so honoured looks so bitter. Kirk lets them wonder and answers their civil tries at talk with icy single words. His first sight of Nemar from the ship does nothing to cool his anger. Smith builds the tale on the gap between the honour of the post and the man's sense of exile.
59733-prince-eugene-the-noble-knight:
George P Upton translated this life of Prince Eugene of Savoy from the German of L Würdig, published at Chicago in 1910. The book belongs to a series of life stories for young people. Four illustrations include the hero of Zenta as frontispiece.

Upton's preface tells the arc. Eugene was meant for the Church, but Louis the Fourteenth refused him a commission in the French army. The slighted young man went to Austria instead and rose to be one of the great generals of his age. For more than fifty years he was in the field. Speed, dash, and personal courage won his battles against larger forces. The life is told as a lesson for youth.
60458-midnight:
Rutherford Montgomery wrote this animal story, copyrighted in 1940, about a creature of the wild called Midnight. A sketch of the author tells his bent: he would rather write than do anything else, and most of his books treat animals and the wilderness. As a boy in North Dakota he listened to hunters' tales; as a man he sat quiet on a log, a watcher, not a hunter.

Montgomery taught school ten years in Wyoming and Colorado, flew in the First World War, and served as a county judge. His other books include Gray Wolf, Yellow Eyes, and Kildee House. He dedicates this one to a friend who knows the value of lonesome places. Young readers who love true-to-life animal tales are his audience.
60713-counterweight:
Counterweight, by Jerry Sohl, is a science fiction story from Worlds of If. It ran in the November 1959 issue, the note on the text says. Keith Ellason, a newsman, is tapped to ride a colony ship as observer. The Weblor One disaster hangs over the offer from the start of talks.

That first ship left with a thousand families for the planet Antheon. Under five hundred colonists lived to land, after revolt split the voyage apart. Captain Sessions bullying fanned chaos among passengers and crew in space. Interstellar wants facts this time, not the garbled crew report of old. Ellason weighs two years in a sardine can against history in the making.
61826-beyond-light:
Nelson Bond wrote Beyond Light, a science fiction story printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1940. Venus was civilized, so the universe thought. But deep in its midnight caverns, beyond light and beyond the wildest imaginings of an ordered system, dwelt horror. The tale opens in the tiny observation turret of the ship Orestes, where Mallory holds a girl close, exactly as bull-voiced Captain Lane finds them, a few thousand miles from Venus.

The captain demands to know what this means, and Mallory answers fast, hoping a soft answer will turn aside wrath. Bond builds pulp menace under a settled Venus. The story mixes shipboard romance with cavern horror.
61834-the-city-of-dreadful-night:
The City of Dreadful Night is a set of sketches of Calcutta by Rudyard Kipling. Grosset published it in New York in 1899. Farrand drew the illustrations. Eight chapters carry the reader through the city. Their titles run from A Real Live City to a chapter concerning a woman named Lucia.

The first chapter salutes Calcutta in the dawn. Kipling calls its exiled Englishmen backwoodsmen beyond the ditch. They have lost their heritage of London, he writes. Its theatres and streets belong to the men at home. Calcutta offers false hopes of return. Later chapters walk the banks of the Hugli. One rides with the Calcutta police. The title chapter descends into the city's night depths.
61840-the-running-fight:
William Hamilton Osborne published The Running Fight in New York in 1910, after his earlier novel The Red Mouse. Pictures by Harrison Fisher and George Brehm run through the book. The front plate shows a young woman urging a man that one stroke of a pen will free her father, which sets the stakes at once.

The story opens with a slight girl at the center of a hard fight that runs through the plot. Osborne writes in the brisk style of the popular novel of his day, with love, money, and family honor in play. Readers get a period tale of pressure and pursuit, where a signature, a father, and a young couple's fate hang together.
62382-thralls-of-the-endless-night:
Leigh Brackett wrote Thralls of the Endless Night for Planet Stories in the fall of nineteen forty-three. The Ship holds an ancient secret, the blurb promises, that means life to dying castaways of the void. Wes Kirk reveals that secret to his people's enemies. His betrayal, the blurb warns, means death to the girl he loves.

Wes Kirk shuts his teeth hard and turns his back on his family. Ma Kirk and the five younger ones huddle around a box of heat-stones. He shoves aside a curtain of little skins at the door. Cold wind threads across his naked feet as he stares out. I would like to kill the Captain, he says carefully, and the officers with him. Brackett's crashed colonists have gone half savage.
62669-the-castle-of-twilight:
Margaret Horton Potter wrote this historical romance, The Castle of Twilight, published at Chicago in 1903 with six pictures. She dedicates it to the friend whose music suggested the story, and a Grieg nocturne is printed near the front. The chapters move by mood: the desolation of age, the silence of youth, then Flammecoeur, the passion, and shadows. A lost Lenore haunts the middle of the book.

Later chapters bring a trumpet call, a storm, a wanderer, and a rising tide. Plates show the castle folk bidding their lord God-speed and a mother and child happy in a flower-strewn meadow. Potter's foreword owns the book a simple story, wistful against the charge of wooden historical fiction. It is a dreamy Breton tale of love across generations, told like music.
62714-the-house-of-delight:
House of Delight is a book for young readers by Gertrude Chandler Warner, copyrighted in 1916. Pilgrim Press of Boston issued the little book with pictures arranged by the author. John Carpenter Warner photographed the illustrations for his kinswoman volume. A caption asks about Alice blue suits trimmed with white braid in the front picture.

Warner dedicates the book to her grandfather, her best playmate in childhood years. That tender note sets the tone of a house made glad by children. Dressing, play, and home joys fill the slight, pictured pages for girls. Warner later won lasting fame with the Boxcar Children books for the young.
63729-in-the-garden-of-delight:
L H Hammond remembers a childhood in In the Garden of Delight, from Thomas Y Crowell Company of New York, copyrighted in 1916. Hammond had written The Master-Word and In Black and White. The book is dedicated to Lucy and Caldwell, in memory of the wheeled-chair summer at Pen-y-Bryn.

The contents run from A Country Child and Bird Corners through premonitions, spring magic, and blackbird diplomacy to the garden of delight itself. The narrator recalls Cedarhurst, where she climbed trees and tore frocks while Great-aunt Virginia and Great-aunt Letitia both looked the other way. Out-of-doors, she says, nothing can spoil.
63807-the-great-green-blight:
The Great Green Blight is a science fiction story by Emmett McDowell, printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1945. Its premise is stark: Earth's empire is crumbling, space liners fall to phantom crews, a green wave of terror spreads, and the few men who could stop it cannot move without dying. Aboard the super space liner Jupiter, young Norman Saint Clair boards with his identity book of photograph, fingerprints, and history, as the rules now demand.

Ships on the Earth to Jupiter run have been vanishing without trace, and neither the Terran Navy nor its intelligence service can find them. The Jupiter carries radium and rates an escort, which does not calm Saint Clair's fear at the last gong. McDowell's tale is space opera of the pulp kind, built on dread, convoys, and an unseen enemy.
63963-mercy-flight:
Mack Reynolds wrote a short space tale that first ran in Planet Stories in July 1951. News men Ed Kerry and Jake get a call from Oneonta. A man is flying in from Luna with a sick child. The child has burns from rays and needs a hospital fast. Jake thinks the tale is old news at first.

Then Ed adds that the ship's radio is broke. That flaw turns a plain mercy flight into a race with no guide. Out in space, a crew in a jam must rely on self alone. The tale builds stress from that one hard fact.
64107-christmas-in-sweden-or-a-festival-:
Sarah Gertrude Pomeroy wrote Christmas in Sweden, or A Festival of Light, issued in Boston in 1911. Dana Estes and Company published it, with drawings by Bertha Hoxie. The story follows an American family to Sweden for a year. Professor Edgecombe wins a post there for his year of rest from teaching.

A telegram brings the news at breakfast one spring morning. His wife and his children, Dorothy and John, will all go with him. He is to render old Norse tales from a document held in Sweden. The family settles there for the winter, so Swedish customs fill the tale. The title points to the feast of light at the heart of the Swedish Christmas season.
64448-happy-rain-night:
Dean Evans sets a tale on Mars on the eve of the yearly synthi-rain, drawn from Planet Stories for March 1954. All Mars settles down for the big sleep that comes with the rain, and traffic thins at a lone fuel port outside the city. The attendant thinks of closing early, near eleven, when no craft has called for ten minutes.

An old, hull-worn ship bangs down into the first cradle, with a wild-haired woman at the controls. She studies a scanning disc, ignores the offer of fuel, then changes her mind when a Security ship settles beside her. She asks the way to Fraon, the gambler's paradise, and lifts off hard for the city. Readers get noir manners in a Martian port, with rain, sleep, and trouble all due at once.
64516-temptress-of-planet-delight:
Temptress of Planet Delight is a science fiction story by a writer named Curtis, printed in Planet Stories in May 1953. A verse at the head tells of a sears-monkey who flew to sell his wares on a strangely groomed planet, and lost all his cares as a genetic experiment bloomed. Herl Hofner, the traveling salesman, is a strapping six-foot man who leaves his ship's little gym when the air signal sounds.

His ship, the Krylla, asks leave to land, calling itself a class M-for-Mary craft. The planet answers with a beam band, and Herl centers his needle and spreads the wings. Later talk tells of far-flung planets left alone for forty years, where much can happen. One past call found a strange change that left half the people deaf and dumb.
64797-the-oversight:
The Oversight, by Breuer, appeared in the magazine Comet in December 1940. John Hastings, a senior medical student at Omaha, drives along the bluff road with Celestine Newbury. In the middle of the Missouri River he sees a Roman galley, sweeping downstream on three tiers of huge oars. His first thought is that his mind is slipping from overwork.

A psychiatry class had lately touched on hysterical delusions. But Celestine sees the galley too, and hears the oar drum and the chanting. The vessel is clumsy, built of heavy timbers, with a high beaked prow and a red and yellow sail. Shields and swords gleam on its crowded decks. Breuer builds his tale on such impossible sightings, which his characters call oversights: things overlooked by time itself.
65374-overlord-of-colony-eight:
Robert Silverberg wrote this tale of a world of green, first printed in a journal of such tales in October 1957. A note at the head gives the sting of the plot. Reese came back to the colony in hope of a glad meet with old friends. In their place he found those friends set to hunt him down like a beast of an alien kind. The tale opens as Jim Reese nears Colony Eight on the world Damballa.

The colony is a huddle of low domes of a stuff like glass, set in a clear space in the wild growth. It is the most glad sight Reese has seen in a month. In that month he had fought with Lois and struck out through the wilds on his own.
65720-the-place-of-animals-in-human-thou:
The Place of Animals in Human Thought is a comparative religion study by the Countess Evelyn Martinengo Cesaresco, printed by Scribner at New York in 1909. A frontispiece shows the Emperor Akbar directing the tying up of a wild elephant, from a tempera painting of 1597. A saying of Berthelot stands as motto: we know nothing except in fragments.

The chapters range across faiths. The faith of Iran and Zoroastrian zoology come early. A religion of ruth, lines from the Adi Granth, and the Hebrew conception of animals follow. Later chapters treat a people and their beasts people by people, creed by creed. Cesaresco asks one question everywhere: what did men think the animal was, and what did they owe it? The book is an early, wide-ranging essay in the history of human kindness and cruelty toward beasts.
65729-john-harper-s-insight:
Dick Purcell wrote John Harper's Insight, a science fiction tale printed in Imagination in October 1956. The head note poses the question plainly, can the mind breach time. Harper was sure he had caught a news item that would change his life, but ironically he caught only a part of it.

They thought he was insane, the tale opens, and with good reason. A man who has spent his life in a machine shop comes down one morning with a wild claim, said in all sincerity. Purcell builds the story on that gap between a glimpse of the future and the proof no one will grant. Readers get a neat, sad tale of foresight without power.
65790-under-the-tiger-s-claws-or-a-strug:
Under the Tiger's Claws, or A Struggle for the Right, is number 436 of the Magnet Library, a weekly of detective literature dated March 21, 1905. Nicholas Carter is the named author, a house name of Street and Smith of New York. His other titles crowd the page: The Great Enigma, Hounded to Death, The Price of a Secret, and Sealed Orders among them.

The contents open with the man and the money, then where tides meet. The tiger's claws, a friend in need, and a turn of luck follow. A startling sequence and the wages of sin pace the case. Nick Carter, the detective of the story, was the most read sleuth in America in the dime novel years. This number puts him against a tiger of a villain in human shape. The Magnet Library sold detection at five cents a week.
66226-overweight-and-underweight:
Overweight and Underweight is a health booklet issued by the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company of New York. The hosted edition is dated January nineteen fifty three, with copyright in nineteen fifty. A contents page starts with the question of what desirable weight is. Dangers of overweight come next, then what makes a person fat.

Why people overeat, how to lose weight, and the body's need for food and exercise fill the middle pages. Short cuts are weighed and calorie tables close the book. Underweight gets its own shorter part on causes and gains. Life insurers sent such guides to policy holders as plain preventive medicine, in firm and friendly tones.
66300-sorrow-in-sunlight:
Sorrow in Sunlight is a novel by Ronald Firbank, published in London by Brentano's in an edition of one thousand numbered copies. Firbank sets his story on a Caribbean island. The opening scene hangs in a lethargic noontide under a giant silk-cotton tree.

Miss Miami Mouth gapes up into the boughs, gloriously bored. Snoring sounds from the cane fields, and the sea shines through the greenery like a floor of silver glass. Her boy Bamboo is out fishing somewhere on it. Her mother dreams of leaving the village of Mediavilla for the capital, which would mean leaving Bamboo behind. Firbank's light, oblique manner was already fully formed in scenes like this one. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
66699-martyr-s-flight:
Hank Searls wrote this science fiction story for a magazine called Imagination, where it ran in December nineteen fifty-five. The scene is Space Station One, in orbit far above the earth. Cargo ships swing down through the air and climb back, and the men aboard count the days until they see their wives.

Colonel Mel Cramer has the hard job of guarding the station if an attack comes. Walter Stanton watches a cargo ship leave and feels the pull of home at Sandia Base. Cramer plans to take his fighter ship out and drill at docking runs, called marriages in station slang. The story turns on duty, risk, and what a guard may be called to give.
66782-nick-carter-stories-no-141-may-22-:
Nick Carter Stories number 141 is a weekly dime novel issue dated May 1915. Street and Smith of Seventh Avenue, New York, issued the stories at five cents. Terms offer one year of the weekly at two dollars and fifty cents, postage free. This number carries The Duplicate Night as its Carter case of the week.

Nick Carter, the great detective of the dime novels, anchors the long running series. Duplicate identities and night work are promised by the title in pulp style. Subscription tables and money order rules fill the front pages for boy buyers. American cheap fiction history keeps Nick Carter as its detective king.
66973-international-thought:
John Galsworthy's International Thought is a sixpenny pamphlet printed by Heffer of Cambridge in 1923. Galsworthy's note on the title page gives all profit from its sale to the League of Nations Union. Its text opens with the sentence the whole essay argues: the exchange of international thought is the only possible salvation of the world.

The essay begins in disenchantment. Those who believed, up to 1914, in civil behaviour between man and man were caught napping by the war and its peace. The rest of mankind, Galsworthy says, felt no astonishment: the doing-down of man by man was daily life, and done collectively it seemed natural. Average life is a long fight, he writes, and justice and co-operation only soften a ruthless contest. The loss falls heaviest because the disenchanted few were the nerves and voice of the community, its poets and teachers.
67720-women-of-ninety-eight:
Mrs Thomas Concannon wrote lives of the women of the Irish rising of 1798. M H Gill and Son issued Women of Ninety-Eight at Dublin in 1919. Concannon had written a life of St Columba and A Garden of Girls. A portrait of Pamela, wife of Lord Edward Fitzgerald, fronts the book.

She gives the work to all dead and living women who gave loved ones to Ireland. Parts treat mothers, wives, and sisters of the famed men of the year. Wolfe Tone's wife, Sarah Curran, and Anne Devlin each get close study. Readers gain the rising retold through grief, loyalty, and hidden courage.
67900-in-the-dead-of-night:
McIntyre wrote In the Dead of Night, a mystery novel printed at Philadelphia in 1908, with pictures by Frances Rogers. It opens on a November night when the pulse of Broadway beats heavily. Its hero, Kenyon, meets a girl in a hansom cab and is drawn step by step into a maze.

A dark house in Selden's Square, strange dangers, and the Bellevue Hospital puzzle deepen the case. A small white hand darts over a shoulder in the frontispiece scene. McIntyre wrote swift, twisty tales of New York by night, and this one runs on secrets, pursuits, and faces half seen in the gaslight. It is a neat sample of the pre-war American mystery.
68326-history-of-electric-light:
Henry Schroeder wrote a history of electric light for the Smithsonian Institution, printed at Washington on August 15, 1923, as volume seventy six, number two of its miscellaneous collections. A chronology of electric light stands near the front. Early records of electricity and magnetism open the tale, then machines making electricity by friction and the Leyden jar.

Electricity from chemical means, Volta's battery improved, and Davy's discoveries follow. The work of Oersted, Ampere, Schweigger, and Sturgeon, Ohm's law, and the invention of the dynamo fill the next pages. Daniell's and Grove's batteries, Grove's showing of incandescent lighting, and early lamps lead toward trade use. Russian lamp makers and the Jablochkoff candle stand in the list. Schroeder gives a plain, dated record of how the electric lamp grew up.
68889-a-history-of-social-thought:
History of Social Thought, by Emory Bogardus, surveys how men have viewed society. The University of Southern California Press issued the book in nineteen twenty two. Bogardus led the sociology and social work department at that university. He gives the book to his students in a warm dedication page.

Chapters start with the nature and earliest forms of social thought. Hebrew, Greek, and Roman thought follow, with Plato and Aristotle treated apart. Early Christian and medieval thought lead on to More and utopian plans. Later chapters treat Malthus, Comte, Marx, Buckle, and Spencer in turn. Ward, eugenic thought, and clash and accord theories close the survey.
69587-the-quenchless-light:
The Quenchless Light is a set of stories by Agnes Laut, published in New York with copyright in 1923 and 1924. Its contents call the tales stories of the apostles' lives. They show the first believers' bold fight to plant the new faith in a dying world, by her account.

Five long tales fill the main book, from Neither Bond Nor Free to a closing promise of no more death. A large appendix follows, on Paul's missionary tours and disputed points. Other notes treat the Herod family, the fall of Jerusalem, and the legend of Thecla. A glad song heads the volume. Readers get vivid biblical fiction backed by study.
69633-jungle-night:
William Beebe published Jungle Night in nineteen eighteen as one of his Atlantic essays on wild life. The essay follows a night hunt on foot in the jungle. Beebe walks behind his Akawai hunter, a quick and quiet man he calls Nupee.

The two men seek kinkajous and giant armadillos in the dark. Beebe notes each sound, each shift of light, and the feel of the forest at night. He also watches his guide with care and warmth. New duties as hunter for the trip weigh on the guide, whose home life Beebe sketches. Close sight and clear prose make the night walk vivid.
69684-red-blight:
Mary Lamar Knight wrote Red Blight, issued in Los Angeles in nineteen fifty-one. Lorrin L Morrison published it in paper and cloth that June. Extra copies could be ordered through a Christian Nationalist Crusade office in St Louis. Knight dedicates it to all who would make freedom's lure irresistible.

False promises of security, she argues, are the bait of communism. Her author's note owns that the views are one person's alone. They rest, she says, on what she herself had seen and learned. The book is a Cold War polemic against the red idea. Knight writes as a warning voice to her fellow Americans. Faith, freedom, and vigilance are her answers.
69865-north-by-night:
North by Night is a Civil War novel by Peter Burchard. Coward-McCann published it in New York in 1962. Burchard dedicated it to a captain of the Seventh Connecticut. An author's note explains the book's basis in fact. The story opens on Saint Helena Island in July 1863.

Its hero, Timothy Bradford, follows that captain's real experiences. The regiment joined a force sent to seize the Carolina sea islands. They made their base at Hilton Head. The book describes the first charge on Fort Wagner. Burchard calls Wagner the strongest earthwork of modern war. A second charge failed a week later. Siege reduced the fort by September. The first chapter opens on a pier with two Yankee soldiers.
69938-told-in-the-twilight:
Weatherly wrote verses for children, issued in New York by Dutton and Company with pictures by Ellen Edwards and John Staples. The book takes its name from the hour at dusk when the sun's last red fades to gray. Weatherly calls that hour the children's own, when dreams come true.

Rhymes cover a dream trial under the sea, a lost lamb, a poet and a printer, and the sums of a girl named Minnie. A dead rabbit, a proud kitten, a cat's own speech, and a lesson for a dog named Toby fill the middle pages. Songs, holly, and a bunch of flowers close the set.
70364-and-there-was-light:
Lester del Rey wrote this science fiction tale, printed in a July 1951 magazine. Its tagline warns that when the enemy believes the worst of you, they will settle for nothing except the worst. The hero, Johann Volcek, believes his new weapon will be humane.

Volcek's invention is meant to be less destructive than the dreaded fusion bombs. His wife Stefanie, still white and weak after losing their child, hurries about their small apartment trying to seem normal as a fateful meeting nears. Del Rey turns the arms race inward, onto one marriage and one conscience. Readers get a quiet, grim tale of the first atomic decade.
70541-star-bright:
Bryce Walton wrote Star Bright for Science Fiction Quarterly in May 1951. Artificial dreams were not enough for Andy Brooks, its headnote says: he was determined to find them in reality. Brooks stands on the balcony of a workers' center apartment, hating his wife's face, and looks at the moon.

In his sensory-show adventures he fought beside a lost sea for the love of the most beautiful actress of the studio city. Reality gives him the Palisades, a tired marriage, and dreams by subscription. Walton, a steady hand in the postwar magazines, writes the dream-machine story as a marriage story. The brightness of the title belongs to the screen, and Brooks's hunger for the real thing drives the trouble.
70675-chicago-by-day-and-night:
Chicago by Day and Night, billed as the pleasure seeker's guide to the Paris of America, was published in Chicago in 1892 by Thomson and Zimmerman. The book runs to 300 pages with 69 pictures. It promises frank advice for a stranger who wants to see the city and stay out of trouble.

Early chapters rate hotels and describe theatres, music halls, and churches. Later ones warn about traps, gambling rooms, and women who cheat new arrivals. Notes on parks, shops, baths, cab fares, and street rules round out the tour. The guide is both a sales pitch for Chicago fun and a warning about its risks.
70817-scream-at-midnight:
Joseph Payne Brennan gathers nine horror tales in a book from his own Macabre House at New Haven, Connecticut. The copyright page dates to 1963. His earlier tale sets, Nine Horrors and a Dream among them, are listed first.

The Horror at Chilton Castle opens the book. Its narrator tours Ireland hunting his Brennan ancestors of Ossory. The family lost its estates under Strafford, who was later beheaded. England follows, then the road north to Chilton Castle. A distant thread ties him to the Chilton-Paynes, earls there. The other tales bear plain, cold titles: The Midnight Bus, The Vampire Bat, Killer Cat, The Dump. Brennan wrote for the pulp magazines and then for small presses. His quiet, literary horror earned a lasting cult.
71380-soldiers-of-the-light:
Soldiers of the Light is a book of poems by Helen Gray Cone, printed in Boston by Richard G Badger at the Gorham Press in 1911, under a 1910 copyright. Many poems had stood in the Century Magazine, the Churchman, the Atlantic Monthly, and Scribner Magazine.

The title poem opens the book, then the Third Day at Gettysburg. Abraham Lincoln, February 12, 1909, and Greencastle Jenny, a ballad of sixty three, follow. By the Blockhouse on the Hill, a ballad of ninety eight, and the Admiral Story stand next. Death after War, the Riddle of Wreck, the Common Street, and Calnan Christmas fill the mid list. A verse asks why she sings of war, she who loves peace of roses in a rain sweet garden. Verse fans get war memory in song.
71497-our-polar-flight:
Roald Amundsen and Lincoln Ellsworth told of their polar flight with fellow crew members. Dodd, Mead and Company held the rights in New York in 1925. Photos taken on the trip fill the book throughout. Two planes, marked N 24 and N 25, form the heart of the bid.

Parts come from the navigator, from a crew diary, and from the weather man. The diary runs from May 21 to June 18, while the crews wait on the ice. Moving 300 tons of ice by hand marks their fight to fly again. Readers gain a full, tense record of skill and grit near the Pole.
72021-the-dark-night:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote The Dark Night, a tale for the young put out at Philadelphia in 1871. Its short title is a line from the old book: the fear of man brings a snare. Guernsey had told tales of Nelly and of Irish Amy in past years. A plate shows Osric as he straps his books in a bunch.

The tale opens on a fine spring dawn in the last days of May. Osric Dennison and his sister Elsie get set for school at Boonville. The school lies near a mile from the home of their father. A short path across lots cuts that span for the pair. Work calls at the red farm house, from corn to wash to the care of pigs and fowls.
72067-between-the-dark-and-the-daylight:
Between the Dark and the Daylight, a science fiction story by David Hodgkins, was printed in Infinity in October 1958. Dan Adkins supplied the illustrations. All they wanted was to see their own children, the headnote says. How could Brendan refuse? Brendan's office sits inside a curved dome wall, twenty feet thick, with rusty rods poking through damp concrete.

Seepage drips without pause, and a thin white mist drifts near the mildew spotted floor. Heating coils buried in the concrete fight the cold. One red lamp glows on Brendan's desk, below the eye level of the half dozen men facing him. The heavy door is barred shut, as Brendan insists for every room. The men have chosen Falconer to speak for them. They tell Brendan he is in charge, but nothing gives him the power to be an autocrat.
72081-the-wizard-of-light:
David Ely wrote The Wizard of Light, a science fiction story printed in Amazing Stories in March 1962, with pictures by Adkins. The head note compares its hero to Samson: to destroy the culture-mongers, Dr Browl needs only a monstrous easel. Browl is an old, very rich man whose tour of the art museums has become a standing joke among the polite men who run them.

They hide their mirth because his money makes him too big to laugh at openly, and he might still buy. Ely sets up a clash between wealth, taste, and the art world's pride. The story is a short satire in science fiction dress.
72172-title-fight:
William Gault wrote this science fiction story for Fantastic Universe in December 1956. Robots were coming up in the world, the blurb complains at the front of the tale. Nick Nolan would show them, getting too big for their britches as they were, it promises in pulp style.

In every robot brain sat a remote-controlled circuit breaker, the editor's note explains. In every robot brain sat also resentment and the plan to work for the day, it adds. Sounds from above lay dim in the dressing room as the tale opens, under tons of robot-made concrete, while a human fighter waits to face a robot in the ring.
72782-as-a-thief-in-the-night:
Austin Freeman wrote this detective novel around his scientific investigator Thorndyke. His name runs through the chapter list: Thorndyke speaks bluntly, Thorndyke challenges the evidence, Thorndyke retraces the trail, and Thorndyke finds the final proof. The narrator is Rupert Mayfield, a friend of the house where the trouble falls.

The opening chapter, The Invalid, brings the Reverend Amos Monkhouse down from his Yorkshire parish to visit his frail brother Harold. The invalid's health has its ups and downs and now sits below its average. Harold's wife Barbara is away in Kent on a political expedition for women's emancipation, which the narrator privately thinks claims attention owed to her sick husband. A shock for the mourners, a verdict, a search warrant, and a Greek gift follow in the contents, with Superintendent Miller puzzled midway.
72812-port-sunlight:
Port Sunlight is a record of a model industrial village by Raffles Davison. Batsford issued the book in London. Its subtitle limits it to the artistic and pictorial side. The preface opens with a bold claim. Everyone has heard of Port Sunlight, it says. Few, though, hold a just estimate of the place. The pages aim to record its best features.

The village was built for the workers of a great soap firm. Its founder's aim sprang from care for workers' well-being. Davison praises the breadth of vision behind the scheme. Cottages, gardens, and a church fill his plates. He predicts the design will win full honour in time. He also says it will be widely copied. Model villages were a live topic then. This book is both record and advertisement of one.
72893-captain-fly-by-night:
Johnston McCulley wrote a west tale of a bold night flyer chief. The book came out in New York in 1926. McCulley wrote The Rangers' Code in his past work. He gave this book to his own girl, Maurine, in front. A new hand drops a cup to start the wild tale.

On the road, dark hints, and a coyote's howl build the front. Two good Samaritans and guests fill the mid parts in line. Two talks and a shaft, then a victor's flight, mark the turns. The call to arms, a ban, and the Presidio stand in the list. A sad turn, an ear at the wall, and a bare face close it. West fans get pace.
73134-through-by-daylight: Through By Daylight is a boys' book in the American Boys' Series, a line of uniform cloth volumes sold at a dollar each. The surviving head of the text is the publisher's series catalogue rather than the story itself. The catalogue promises thoroughly American tales by favourite boys' authors of the day, among them Oliver Optic, Elijah Kellogg, and James de Mille. Sea, lake, island, and school adventures fill the list around this title, each volume complete in itself and newly priced within reach of all.
73146-forbidden-flight:
Chester B Conant launches young rocketeers on a banned voyage in a tale from Future combined with Science Fiction, October 1941. The piece is billed as a future fiction brief.

The Junior Rocketeers were founded late in the twenty-first century. The Board of Interuniversal Transportation set them up to stir youth toward space. Young pilots poured in from all walks of life. The Tellurian Army of Maintenance drew officers from their ranks. Now a crew of six rides in silence, reliving the past months. Doctor Henry Neist rises to plead the cause of sanity. The hurt eyes around him show what his plea will cost. Conant writes in the earnest mode of early science fiction, when rocket clubs were real and space felt one bold step away.
73196-too-dearly-bought:
Too Dearly Bought, or The Town Strike, by Agnes Giberne, was printed in London. Shaw issued the tale among her stories for home libraries. Review lines call it a timely story that should spread widely. Fourteen chapters make up the book. It opens with flags and banners in Pleasant Lane. A procession of strikers comes down the lane, led by noisy small boys. Wives and mothers turn out at their doors to watch.

Chapter heads name Peter Pope's speech and Holdfast's speech. A ducking, the children, and baby Harry mark the middle. Cold evenings and hard talks show the strike's cost at home. Another meeting and a discussion lead to the close. Giberne writes a moral tale of labour strife for family readers.
74155-a-frontier-knight:
A Frontier Knight is a story of early Texan border life by Amy Blanchard. It was copyrighted in 1905 and illustrated by Stecher. The first chapter is set at the old Kentucky home, under bright sun on blue-grass meadows. Chapters follow Fidgetty Lou, a chase, and the start off to war.

Alison, the heroine, has adventures in the dead of night and makes discoveries with Hannah Maria. A raffle, Lou's wedding, and a clue carry the middle of the tale. Neal's letter and a norther storm raise the close. The return of Sir Artegall and new homes end the book. Blanchard wrote many such wholesome tales for girls.
74428-straight-forward-or-walking-in-the:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote Straight Forward, or Walking in the Light, as a story for school girls. Henry Hoyt of Boston entered it under copyright in 1859. Guernsey had written Irish Amy and other tales for the young. Her heroine is a schoolgirl also named Lucy.

Lucy refuses a pretty set of tablets priced at a dollar. She cannot afford them, though the shopman offers credit with a smile. Her friend Emily, who also has no money, lets the cost go on a bill. Gloves, laces, and embroidery tempt the party at the next shop. The tale turns on small choices about debt, truth, and self-rule. Guernsey makes a shopping trip carry a lesson her readers were meant to carry for life.
746-burning-daylight:
Jack London wrote this novel about Elam Harnish, called Burning Daylight, a prospector who burns his life like daylight in the Yukon gold fields. He wins and loses fortunes at cards and claims, living hard among men who talk of scurvy cures in a quiet saloon. His energy and luck make him a legend of the north.

Daylight later turns to business in California, where he finds that city wealth brings a different kind of risk. London follows his hero from camp to boardroom, asking what a strong man is worth when gold is no longer the prize. The novel blends adventure with a critique of finance, and it shows London's power as a storyteller of the wild.
74732-on-the-theory-of-the-infinite-in-m:
On the Theory of the Infinite in Modern Thought is a pair of lectures by Jourdain of Oxford. Longmans issued the book in London in 1911. Jourdain was vice-principal of Saint Hugh's Hall. The first lecture dates from 1905. It was given to women students of science at Oxford. The second, on pragmatism, dates from 1908. Her brother helped prepare the text for print.

The first study treats the finite and the infinite. It asks how mathematics bears on philosophy. Kant held that number rests on time and space, she notes. New logic instead grounds number in the laws of thought. From simple bases the mind builds complex ones. The second study joins this to a theory of knowledge. The lectures open a hard subject to general hearers. They keep the spoken form of the hall.
75076-an-interrupted-night:
Isabella Alden, who wrote under the name Pansy, began this tale, and her niece Grace Livingston Hill put it in final shape. The book came out in 1929, when Alden was eighty-seven years old and confined to bed. Hill explains in the preface that the tale rests on true facts told by the woman shown in the story as a Mrs Dunlap.

The story tells how a young girl meets one of the most terrible trials life can bring. With help from an older woman, she faces the night that changes her life. Alden's books were loved for their warmth and faith. Readers get her last tale, finished with care by a niece who knew her well.
75393-was-i-right:
Was I Right is a tale by Mrs Walton for the Religious Tract Society. The society put the book out from Paternoster Row in London town. Walton had writ Christie's Old Organ and Peep Behind the Scenes. Nineteen chapters run from the two letters to the title question asked again. A picture at the manor house fronts the book.

My choice, was I wrong, and Maggie's aunts fill the early list. Alliston Hall, conscience at work, and Alice Fitzgerald follow in order. Was the promise binding and Evelyn's confession crowd the mid chapters. Brindisi, Jerusalem, and Sunday on Mount Zion carry the tale abroad. The mystery solved and my olive-leaves lead to the final asking. In anxious moments we notice every little object, the teller opens. One day stands out in her life above all others to remember. She sees herself at nineteen on that day.
75628-in-the-night:
In the Night is a novel by R Gorell Barnes, published by Longmans, Green and Company in 1917. The story is set in Salting, a small farming village a mile or two from a branch railway line, where talk runs on seasons, crops, and neighbours.

Above the village stands Salting Towers, home of Sir Roger Penterton, a retired businessman who cares nothing for the place below his hill. The opening chapter gathers labourers in the bar of the Rose and Crown as dusk settles on the fields. Barnes builds the book on the gap between the great house and the village that ignores it back. The contents list a late chapter called Sight at Last, hinting at blindness, literal or otherwise, resolved near the end.
76397-where-the-battle-was-fought:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote a novel of Tennessee in the wake of the Civil War. Ticknor and Company issued the fifth form at Boston in 1886. Rights were held in 1884 by James R Osgood and Company. Craddock had written In the Tennessee Mountains, as the title page notes.

An old battlefield in Tennessee is said to be haunted in peacetime. Bugle calls, drum rolls, and ghost hosts trouble fireside groups at night. By day the plain lies gray, with rows of once-used graves in its thickets. No pay can make a ploughman break that turf, the tale says, and lives unfold in its shade.
76806-the-law-of-copyright:
The Law of Copyright prints, for private circulation in 1916, the poet William Wordsworth's open letter on copyright to Serjeant Talfourd. The prefatory note dates it. The bill was presented to the Commons on April 18, 1838, the day the poet addressed his letter. It appeared in the Morning Post of April 23 that year.

The letter had escaped all notice until the editor chanced upon it. Wordsworth argues for a long term of copyright after an author's death, so that a writer's family may live by his work. His own sonnets on the subject were famous; the letter is their prose twin. Talfourd's bill failed, but the cause won ground for a century. Collectors printed this pamphlet in 1916 as a curiosity of the great poet in the lobby. Literature and law meet in it briefly.
77286-the-bridge-of-light:
Hyatt Verrill's Bridge of Light ran in Amazing Stories Quarterly in the fall of 1929, a long tale of a lost world. The narrator, homeward bound from a South American expedition, stops at Vigo in Spain and wanders into the second-hand shops of the old quarter. He carries the proof of his adventure on his body: scars covering his left arm, and a tattooed symbol on his chest. And there is Itza, in a hammock on his porch as he writes, exotic as an orchid.

An illustration shows the heart of the tale: Itza stepping with a contemptuous toss of her head over the verge of a terrible chasm. Verrill was a veteran writer of the South American wilds, and the story mixes his traveler's eye for old Spain with a hidden-world romance. The magazine billed it, simply, as Verrill's best.
77383-photography-self-taught:
Photography Self Taught is a small manual by Lloyd Snodgrass, issued as Little Blue Book Number 1139. Haldeman-Julius edited the series at Girard, Kansas. The copyright is 1926. The contents run in three parts. An introduction treats the simplicity of the art and its early stages. The materials of photography come next: types of cameras, lenses, stops and shutters, films and plates, and printing papers. Making the picture fills the rest.

A box camera, Snodgrass says, is a light-tight box with a lens at one end and film at the other. Such a camera suits a child or a beginner well. There is little to get out of order, and it is ready on the instant. Exposure tables and home portraiture get their pages. The Little Blue Books sold for a few cents to all America.
77604-kings-of-the-night:
Kings of the Night, a tale by Robert Howard, ran in Weird Tales in November 1930. Verses from The Song of Bran head the story, of a Caesar on an ivory throne whose legions came to break a king in a land unknown. The tale opens at a grim altar of the God of Shadows, lit by a single torch in dark trees.

A dagger flashes, a cry breaks in a gasp, and bony fingers tear the heart from a victim's breast as four men watch. One, lithe and keen of face, wears an iron band with a single red jewel. A taller, grey-eyed guest, Cormac of Connacht, stands ill at ease: the Druids of Erin had dark rites, but none like this. Howard mixes Roman Britain, Pictish kings, and horror.
77716-the-cohansey-tea-fight:
The Cohansey Tea Fight is a tale by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, printed as the lead piece of The Atlantic Monthly for April 1874. The Atlantic cost thirty five cents a number and four dollars a year at the time. Guernsey tells the tale in a family voice.

Rain pours down as Violet looks out and asks her aunt if there is any use in thinking of it. The plan is a trip to Annabella Floyd tea fight, a new slang term for a girls tea party. Grandmother Howell asks what a tea fight is, to Aunt Elisabeth horror at the slang. The tale ties the new term to an old one, the tea burning at Greenwich in New Jersey in the Revolution. Readers get a warm tale where a tea party opens a door on the past.
77757-bookbinding-self-taught:
Ben Davidson wrote Bookbinding Self Taught, Little Blue Book number 1192, printed at Girard, Kansas, in 1927. Davidson begins with his own case. He owned several hundred Little Blue Books and had made linen holders for them. The satisfaction of rebinding his torn books led him to write the guide.

Chapters cover the tools and materials, stitching, binding, and rebinding old books. Loose-leaf scrap books and lettering come last. His first project is the simplest: a linen cover for a single Blue Book, with measures given to the fraction of an inch. It is a thrifty, plain book for people who kept small libraries and liked to mend them with their own hands.
78025-main-currents-in-american-thought:
Vernon Louis Parrington wrote Main Currents in American Thought, a reading of American letters from the start to nineteen twenty, and this is volume one. The set's three parts treat the colonial mind, the romantic turn of eighteen hundred to eighteen sixty, and the start of hard eyed realism after that. Volume one runs from sixteen twenty to eighteen hundred. Parrington gave the work to the memory of Allen Smith, a scholar and teacher.

Parrington says he follows the broad path of politics, trade, and social life rather than fine letters alone. He traces seed ideas that came to be counted as truly American, how they arose, and how they were fought. This volume runs from Puritan New England to the triumph of Jefferson and farm democracy. Old world seeds, from English independence to French thought, took root in American soil along the way.
78276-bride-of-the-night:
Louise Gerard wrote Bride of the Night, a novel copyrighted in 1930 and published at New York by the Macaulay Company. She dedicated it to a friend without whose help and constant encouragement, she says, neither this nor any of her books would have been written. An epigraph asks what the wild winds are: love and hate and lust and avarice, blowing through the kingdom of the soul.

Part one opens under another verse: men will call me unrelenting, pitiless, vindictive, stern. Chapter one weighs offences against excuses and asks how to scale the soul of a man. Gerard wrote romance and adventure for a large popular audience between the wars. Her heroines face hard men and harder choices. Bride of the Night is her manner in its title: passion after dark, with a moral reckoning at dawn.
78506-pilgrims-of-the-night:
Pilgrims of the Night, subtitled a study of expelled peoples, was written by Edward E. Swanstrom and published in New York in 1950. Francis Cardinal Spellman wrote the foreword. Swanstrom had seen war torn lands himself and wrote with pity for the people left homeless there.

Chapters take up work, slave labor, women, and children among the displaced. Two more deal with priests and bishops who bore heavy loads. The last chapter views the long line of refugees as a whole. Readers get a first hand, faith based account of the refugee crisis that followed the Second World War.
78700-the-trail-of-the-white-knight:
The Trail of the White Knight is a tale of crime by Bruce Graeme. It first came out in London in the fall of 1920. Fresh prints kept it in the shops for more than ten years. It stands in a cheap set of tales with two of his past books.

The set lists the Palmer and Biggers books by its side for the trade. The tale opens as a talk of love on a warm night in July. Two walk the shade paths of an isle in a great town's stream. The air is sweet with young love in the soft dark of the walk. From that calm start the trail of the knight runs to crime. Graeme's name on the set marks the book as a trade thrill tale.
79109-my-honourbright:
Annette Lyster wrote My Honourbright, a tale printed in London by the National Society's Depository, with two plates by W S Stacey. One plate shows a Dr Musgrave calling on Miriam and Honora. Lyster had written The Fortunes of Peggy Treherne and The White Gipsy.

Early chapters bring Dr Elliott, Miss Vandeleur of S Canice, and a load of family cares. A ruby ring, a second Miss Vandeleur, and a first wedding in the family turn the plot. The tale keeps close to home life, with kin, calls, and courtship at its heart. Readers of church and home fiction in Lyster's day got a clean tale in which duty and love pull against each other page by page.
79143-the-poetry-of-pathos-delight:
Alice Meynell selected The Poetry of Pathos and Delight from the works of Coventry Patmore. William Heinemann published the book in London in 1896. A portrait of Patmore, after a painting by J S Sargent, fronts the volume. Meynell explains in her note that this is not a selection in the usual sense.

She did not hunt for best passages, she says. Instead she gathered places where Patmore deals with two things: delight and sorrow. Those passions, she argues, are ones his poetry touches so closely that it seems to mingle with them. Her hope is to win new readers for the poet's whole work. Patmore's greatest poems, she notes, belong to the last quarter of the century. The book serves as a doorway into a difficult, admired poet.
79582-named-right:
Andrew Caffrey's short story Named Right calls itself a story of the air mail pilots. Pilot Rutter had flown the San Francisco to Reno mail for more than two years, with the route from its start. In all that time he had known hard work and real grief, but he had never once been lost, which came near to a record.

His pal Miller blames luck, yet Rutter regrets the record. A new pilot named Page, fresh from the East, got badly lost twice in his first month and won front pages across America for days. Rutter's joke gives the tale its title. Page, he tells Miller, is surer than anything named right, and Miller answers that envy is eating him.
79642-silver-bird-s-flight:
Silver Birds Flight is a tale of air flight and plots by Gordon Stiles. A front blurb says its pilot tempts fate and falls in a snare of plots. Ray Folsom is the pilot of the great plane named the Silver Bird. Her motor hum at rest is likened to music in his ear.

Ray scans low grey clouds on a Long Island field at the start. A news man asks if the hop can go at dawn the next day. Ray will not guess the sky, but counts on three fair days to come. A rich backer holds the call on when the great flight starts. Air risk and hid schemes form the pull of the pulp tale.
79755-twilight:
Annette Lyster wrote Twilight, a story of two villages, published in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Paget illustrated it. Lyster also wrote Footprints and The White Gipsy. Her story opens in a Yorkshire village lying low on a mountain where a small stream rises. A shallow valley runs across the slope, with a level space at the foot of a steep descent.

The contents join the two villages of the subtitle. Giles Brent comes home to a cottage near the miner's road. Chapters treat turf and coal, a fever mound, a medal, and a hard struggle in the mine. Giles's crutch, a flight, and three happy years follow. Lyster's tale, like her others for the Society, sets mining life and village faith side by side.
8908-the-ignatian-epistles-entirely-spur:
W. D. Killen, a professor of church history in Ireland, published this short work in Edinburgh in 1886. It answers Bishop J. B. Lightfoot, who had defended the letters linked to Ignatius, an early church leader said to have died a martyr. Killen argues that those letters are not genuine at all.

He takes apart the story of Ignatius's death and the style of the letters, and he says they lack the mark of one real man writing last words to real churches. Readers get a sharp look at how scholars of that age tested old texts, and why the fight over seven short letters mattered so much to church history.
9851-love-at-second-sight:
Ada Leverson wrote Love at Second Sight in 1916, the third book of her Little Ottleys series. Edith Ottley, resting on a blue sofa by the fire, starts up at a crash, shrieks, and a quarrel on the stairs. Her son Archie, a handsome boy of ten with clear grey eyes, calmly blames Madame Frabelle for the noise. His sly, reserved glance already hints at public school to come.

The novel follows Edith, Archie, and their circle through comic domestic storms, with Leverson's light, ironic wit. Love, seen twice, proves truer than first sight. A reader gets a witty Edwardian comedy of family life, and a fond return to the Ottleys.
9862-city-of-endless-night:
Milo Hastings wrote City of Endless Night in 1920, a dystopian novel of a future Berlin under black rule. Chapters trace a red, black, and gold struggle on the world's changing map, potash mines at Stassfurt, and a diary in a dead man's pocket. A black utopia breeds its blond brood, while free women drink synthetic beer. The hero is drafted for paternity and petitions a eugenic chief.

Later chapters salute a statue of God, weigh a goddess grown obese, and hear a royal voice answer a talking delegate. Hastings writes with satiric bite. A reader gets a strange, bold future satire, where eugenics, war, and utopia collide.
a-history-of-freedom-of-thought: John Bagnell Bury writes a history of freedom of thought from Greece to modern times. His chapters move from reason free in Greece and Rome to reason in prison in the Middle Ages. The Renaissance, Reformation, toleration, and rationalism bring a prospect of deliverance. Bury, Cambridge professor of modern history, tells how free thought won its ground.
a-queens-delight: An anonymous London compiler gathers the arts of preserving, conserving, and candying in this household book, first printed in 1671. The volume also teaches perfumes and the distilling of excellent waters, beginning with plums preserved in their just weight of sugar. Its recipes scald, steep overnight, boil, and skim with care, offering a queen's delight of conserves, preserves, and sweet waters for a well-ordered still room.
a-thief-in-the-night:
A Thief in the Night, published in 1905 by E W Hornung, collects short stories about A J Raffles, the gentleman thief. Raffles is a prominent member of London society and a national sporting hero, a cricketer who regularly plays for England. He uses that cover to commit burglaries, stealing valuable jewellery from the hosts who welcome him.

At his side works his friend Bunny Manders, younger and idealistic, who narrates their crimes with admiration and nerves. Both men live under the constant surveillance of the police, and each story turns on a theft planned and executed under that watch. The collection is a cornerstone of the Raffles series, the tales that made the amateur cracksman famous.
an-easter-disciple-the-chronicle-of-quin: Arthur Benton Sanford writes An Easter Disciple, the chronicle of Quintus, a Roman knight, in memory of absent ones who have entered into life. The story follows a Roman through the events of Easter, toward faith and new understanding. Sanford's devotional romance joins historical colour with a Christian message.
