The tale suits readers who like faith told through story.
aslauga-s-knight:
Friedrich de la Motte Fouque sets this tale on the Danish island of Funen, where the knight Froda keeps open house for skalds and hunts out old songs and legends. A learned Icelander sends him a painted book: the history of Aslauga, daughter of Sigurd, who kept goats in disguise and then won King Ragnar Lodbrok. Froda reads it before his castle one autumn evening.

The long-dead queen rises so vividly before him that Froda vows himself her knight. It matters nothing to him that a hundred years separate them; she will inspire his battles and his songs. Fouque follows the vow through friendship, a living maiden who bears Aslauga's name and face, and war. The tale asks what a man owes a love that exists only in a book.
between-the-dark-and-the-daylight:
William Dean Howells called these seven tales Romances, publishing them in 1907 under the title Between the Dark and the Daylight. A Sleep and a Forgetting opens the volume: Matthew Lanfear stops at San Remo, between Genoa and Nice, on a friend's errand, and meets a woman who cannot remember him. The Eidolons of Brooks Alford, A Memory That Worked Overtime, and A Case of Metaphantasmia continue the twilight logic.

Editha, the famous story, stands fifth: a girl sends her lover to the Spanish war in a fervour of patriotism and must meet what returns. A sampled confession elsewhere in the volume has a lover begging his beloved not to praise him until she knows his despair as well as his love. Howells works the borderland of mind: dreams, doubles, and second sight handled with a realist's tact.
britannica-1911-absorption-of-light:
Absorption of Light receives a long physics entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Light crossing empty space loses nothing, the entry begins; only spreading thins it. Through matter it always loses some energy, turned to heat or re-emitted at lower frequency.

Even the clearest bodies absorb measurably, and sunset dimming shows air doing it over long paths. Surface governs much: platinum black swallows nearly all light, polished platinum reflects most. Absorptive power names the share of a given wave-length a body takes in, and a perfectly black body stays an ideal. Selective absorption rules most bodies, each favouring certain wave-lengths. Heated bodies emit just what they absorb, so a black-patterned tile glows pattern-bright against its ground.
britannica-1911-agriculture-sale-of-catt:
Weighing a beast, rather than guessing its bulk by eye, is the change urged in Sale of Cattle by Live Weight, a part of the Agriculture article. British markets and fairs had long priced stock by look and touch. The 1891 act on weighing cattle at markets and fairs threw the law's weight behind the weighbridge.

Fairness drove the shift. Butchers bought far more often than graziers did, so their eye for weight grew sharper, and the scales put both sides on one level. Figures for 1905 came from twenty-six listed places in England and ten in Scotland. Fat cattle passed over the bridge far more in Scotland than in England that year. Store cattle, by contrast, were still seldom weighed before a sale.
britannica-1911-aht:
Aht, a confederacy of North American Indian tribes, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The confederacy numbered twenty-two tribes of the Wakashan stock, a language family of the Pacific coast. Its people were settled on the west coast of Vancouver in British Columbia. Together they numbered some 3,500 when the entry was compiled.

Five leading tribes are named out of the twenty-two. They are the Nitinaht, the Tlaasaht or Makah, the Tlaokiwaht or Clahoquaht, the Ahansaht, and the Ehatishaht. The double names in that list reflect the spellings then in use for the same peoples. Short as the notice is, it fixes the confederacy's place, its language stock, its rough size, and the names by which its main member tribes were known to readers of the time.
britannica-1911-barometric-light:
Barometric light is the luminous glow given off by mercury in a barometer tube when the tube is shaken. Jean Picard first observed the effect. It became the subject of many experiments by Francis Hawksbee, whose work fills most of this short entry.

Hawksbee showed that the Torricellian vacuum, the empty space at the top of the tube, is not essential to the glow. The same light appeared when mercury was shaken with air that was only partly rarefied, thinned out. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the cause in one line: the glow is an effect of the electricity generated by friction between the mercury and the air inside the tube.
britannica-1911-bengel-johann-albrecht:
Johann Albrecht Bengel (1687–1752) was a Lutheran divine and scholar born at Winnenden in Württemberg. His father died when he was six, and a family friend schooled him at Stuttgart. At Tübingen from 1703 he read Aristotle and Spinoza in his spare hours, with Spener, Arndt and Franke for theology.

Bengel entered the ministry in 1707 and later headed the theology school at Denkendorf. Doubts over the true reading of Greek New Testament passages, felt early, drove his great work. His edition of the Greek Testament came out in 1734, sorting the old copies into two families. His Gnomon, notes on the New Testament, made his name as an interpreter of Scripture.
britannica-1911-bight:
Bight is an English word for a bend, kin to the German Bucht, a bay, and beugen, to bend. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives the word two working senses. In nautical use, a bight is the loop or bent part of a rope. That loop is set against the rope's ends, which have their own names and uses aboard ship. The word marks the slack middle curve of the line.

In geography, a bight is a bay between two distant headlands. Its curve is shallow rather than deep. The entry names two famous cases as examples. One is the Bight of Benin on the African coast. The other is the Great Bight of Australia, on that continent's southern shore. The entry runs to only a few lines and gives no history of the word's use at sea.
britannica-1911-bitzius-albrecht:
Albrecht Bitzius (1797–1854) was a Swiss novelist, best known by his pet name Jeremias Gotthelf. He was born at Morat on 4 October 1797, where his father was pastor. The family moved to Utzenstorf in the Bernese Emmenthal in 1804. There the boy grew up among village boys and helped on his father's glebe land. He finished his schooling at Bern and was received as a pastor in 1820. A Göttingen visit followed in 1821.

He served as his father's assistant, then settled at Lützelflüh in the Upper Emmenthal. He succeeded its old pastor in 1832 and married the pastor's granddaughter in 1833. He spent the rest of his life in that village, dying in October 1854. His first work, the Bauernspiegel, appeared in 1837. The 1911 Britannica entry covers his tales of peasant life across many volumes. His Whig politics, against the Radicals of 1846, echo in some writings as a slight drawback.
britannica-1911-browne-hablot-knight:
Hablot Knight Browne (1815–1882) was an English artist famed as Phiz. The pen name on his drawings, illustrator of the best-known books by Charles Dickens, Charles Lever and Harrison Ainsworth in their first editions. Of Huguenot extraction, he was born in Lambeth on 11 June 1815. His father died early and left the family badly off, and he was apprenticed to Finden, the noted steel engraver.

Engraving did not suit him at all. A Society of Arts prize in 1833 for a drawing of John Gilpin let him abandon it in 1834 for other art work, aiming at painting. In spring 1836 he met Dickens just when the serial Pickwick was in danger for want of a capable illustrator. As an interpreter of Dickens's characters, the entry judges Phiz in some respects the equal of Cruikshank and Leech.
britannica-1911-carpet-knight:
Carpet-knight is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry defining a term of reproach. Properly, a carpet-knight is a man knighted in peacetime on the carpet before the king's throne. He did not win the honour on the field of battle as a direct reward for valour. The phrase thus marks the gap between honours earned in war and honours granted at court.

The entry explains the sting in the phrase. People used it against a soldier who stays at home and avoids active service with its hardships. The carpet in question points in particular to a lady's chamber, where such an idle soldier lingers instead of campaigning. In a few lines the entry gives both the strict sense of the term and the insult it carried in common use.
britannica-1911-connaught:
Connaught is a province of Ireland on its midwestern coast. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists its counties and old kings. The river Shannon forms most of its eastern border. Mayo, Sligo, Leitrim, Galway, and Roscommon make up the province.

Legend gives the land to a people called the Damnonians. A king list in the Book of Leinster starts in old times. That first dynasty held its own into the fourth century. A high king of the Milesian line then cast it out. Annals stay quiet until a Norman grant near 1200. The Burgh family then bound its fate to the province. Their kin split and took on Irish ways in the wild west. English rule bit deep only in the sixteenth century.
britannica-1911-copyright:
Copyright, in law, is the sole right of an author or his assignees to multiply copies of an original work for sale. It covers works in literature and in art. As a known form of property it is young beside other kinds. Printing made it needful, by the ease it gave to copying. The right in books came first in time, and the right in art works followed in its train.

One great doubt long hung over the right in England. Did the common law own it at all before statute spoke? Blackstone held that such property rests on labour and invention. He tied it to the head of occupancy in law. Yet he spoke with doubt of its sure place. Men of law lined up on both sides of the point. A furniture catalogue case shows in its later pages.
britannica-1911-fleischer-heinrich-leber:
Heinrich Leberecht Fleischer (1801-1888), German Orientalist, was born at Schandau in Saxony on 21 February 1801. From 1819 to 1824 he studied theology and oriental languages at Leipzig, then continued his studies in Paris. In 1836 he became professor of oriental languages at Leipzig University. He kept that chair until his death, a span of more than fifty years in one post. His name rests on his editions and catalogues of eastern texts, in Arabic, Turkish and Persian.

Fleischer's chief works include editions of Abulfeda's history of the time before Islam and of Beidhawi's commentary on the Koran. He catalogued the oriental manuscripts in the royal library at Dresden and in the town library at Leipzig. He edited and translated Ali's Hundred Sayings, finished volumes of the Thousand and One Nights, and edited a Persian grammar. He was one of eight foreign members of the French Academy of Inscriptions. He died at Leipzig on 10 February 1888.
britannica-1911-flugel-gustav-leberecht:
Gustav Leberecht Flugel (1802-1870), German orientalist, was born at Bautzen on 18 February 1802. He had his early schooling at the gymnasium of his native town and studied theology and philology at Leipzig. Gradually oriental languages claimed his whole attention, and he pursued them in Vienna and Paris. In 1832 he became professor at the Furstenschule of St Afra in Meissen. Ill-health forced him to resign in 1850, and in 1851 he moved to Vienna.

At Vienna Flugel catalogued the Arabic, Turkish and Persian manuscripts of the court library. He died at Dresden on 5 July 1870. His chief work is an edition, with Latin translation, of Haji Khalfa's lexicon, in seven volumes. He also edited the Koran and published a concordance to it. He wrote on Mani and on the grammatical schools of the Arabs, among other eastern subjects.
britannica-1911-kirkcudbright:
Kirkcudbright is a royal and police burgh and the county town of Kirkcudbrightshire, Scotland, with 2386 people in 1901. It stands at the mouth of the Dee, 6 miles from the sea. Dumfries lies 30 miles southwest, by the Glasgow and South Western railway. The old form of the name was Kilcudbrit, from the Gaelic for the chapel of Cuthbert.

The saint's body is said to have rested here for a short time in the seven years between its taking up at Lindisfarne and its burial again at Chester le Street. The estuary of the Dee is split at its head by the peninsula of St Mary's Isle. The harbour is the best in southwestern Scotland, though the tide falls back so far that its use is much hindered.
britannica-1911-landsknecht:
A landsknecht was a German foot man for hire of the past age but four. The name means man of the plains, set past the Swiss men of the hills. That Swiss host was then the type of hired foot in all Europe. An emperor raised the new force past the end of that age.

Past two great fights where the Swiss name broke, the new force was held the best foot in Europe. They served as hired bands in scores of lands, on all sides of a war. Their chief arms were long pikes. Their ranks, posts, and camp rules set the mold for the regiments of later hosts, and their name spread in bent forms past all west lands.
britannica-1911-resht:
Resht, the capital of the province of Gilan in Persia, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the left bank of a branch of the White river, which flows into a lagoon of the Caspian shore. The port where ships from Russia land lies fourteen miles away. Since 1892 a small steamboat could cover part of that trip when the water ran deep enough.

The article gives the town 60,000 people and calls it the seat of the governor of the province. Consuls from England, Russia, France, and Turkey lived there. The town sits in low, unhealthy ground and was once buried in jungle. Russian troops cleared much timber during their stay in the years after 1723. Its houses have red tile roofs, are raised off the ground, and carry broad porches with wide eaves.
britannica-1911-spire-light:
Spire lights are the small windows set in a church spire. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the French name for them and states where they occur. They are found in all periods of English Gothic building, and in French spires they form a key part of the whole design.

The entry names an early case in the spire of the great church at Oxford. It notes two traits of the form: the lights are not glazed, and when they are large they may carry cross bars to brace the upright bars of the frame. Short as it is, the piece fixes the term, its range, and its build for readers of church design.
britannica-1911-whitney-william-dwight:
William Dwight Whitney was an American scholar of words who lived from eighteen twenty-seven to eighteen ninety-four. He was born at Northampton in Massachusetts and did well at Williams College. He first worked in field science with his brother on surveys. A new love of Sanskrit then drew him to deep study.

The entry tells of his years in Germany with famed teachers of old tongues. On his return he took the chair of Sanskrit at Yale and later taught the science of speech as well. He won high honours at home and abroad. His prize work on an old Sanskrit text is singled out for praise.
britannica-1911-yarmouth-isle-of-wight:
Yarmouth is a small port at the west end of the Isle of Wight in England. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Solent shore where the Yar river meets the sea. Steam boats link it with Lymington, and a rail line serves the town.

The entry traces the town from the Domesday Survey of ten eighty six. It lists charters from Baldwin de Redvers and from kings who came later. Yarmouth sent members to parliament until the Reform Act of eighteen thirty two. The church holds a fine monument to Admiral Sir Robert Holmes. Readers get a compact past of a small port and its civic rights.
britannica-1911-zaimukht: Zaimukht is the name of a small Pathan tribe on the Kohat border of the North West Frontier Province of India, covered in a short 1911 Britannica note. They live in hills south of the Orakzais, between two valleys. Their land forms a triangle of near four hundred square miles, a fourth of it held by an Orakzai clan. The tribe is called a fine looking, strong race, with a fighting strength of some three thousand men.
burning-daylight:
Jack London named Burning Daylight for its hero, a Klondike miner called Burning Daylight who strikes coarse gold in his pan and becomes a king of the Yukon camps. The opening sits in a Dawson saloon, men arguing scurvy cures while the gambling tables stand idle. Daylight's luck, strength, and appetite make him a legend.

He carries his millions south to California, conquers Oakland and San Francisco finance, and finds the game emptier than the goldfields. Stenographer Dede Mason, whose salary he quietly raises, draws him toward a simpler life on a ranch. London shapes the novel as an argument: wealth burns daylight, while work, land, and love restore it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-utr:
Michael Ott's entry follows Conrad of Utrecht, bishop born in Swabia, killed at Utrecht on 14 April 1099. Before his bishopric he served Cologne's Anno II as chamberlain and Prince Henry, future Henry IV, as tutor. When excommunicated Bishop William died in 1076, the emperor gave Conrad the see. Like his predecessor he sided with Henry IV against Gregory VII, and at Brixen in 1080 condemned the pope as a heretic. Lambert of Hersfeld calls him a schismatic bishop unworthy of his see.

War with Robert of Flanders brought defeat, captivity, and loss of part of South Holland. The emperor compensated with Stavoren in Friesland in 1077, adding Ostergau and Westergau in 1086. Conrad founded Utrecht's collegiate church of Notre-Dame. Shortly after Mass, his discharged Frisian architect assassinated him, possibly at a nobleman's instigation over domains Conrad held unjustly. He reportedly wrote Pro Imperatore contra Papam for Gerstungen's 1085 synod, though Hefele judges Aventinus its author.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lamprecht:
Lamprecht, called Der Pfaffe, the Priest, was a twelfth-century German poet and cleric of whom almost nothing personal survives but his name. His Alexanderlied was the first German secular epic built on a French model.

That model was Alberic de Besancon's poem on Alexander, of which only 105 opening verses survive. Lamprecht followed it fairly closely, adding moralizing and learned remarks, and drew also on the Historia de preliis and an Iter ad paradisum for Eastern marvels and Alexander's journey to Paradise. There entry is refused him, and he learns the emptiness of earthly glory, closing the 7,302 short rhymed couplets in a moralizing tone. The poem was likely written in Middle Rhenish lands about 1130.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monastery-of-:
Tallaght, five miles south of Dublin, takes its Irish name from words for plague and stone monument. The name recalls an early burial ground of the Parthalonians, wiped out by plague in legend. Its monastery was founded by Saint Maelruain, who died in 792. The site was given in honour of God and Saint Michael by Cellach of the Ui Donnchada.

Maelruain's companion Saint Aengus the Culdee helped him compile the Martyrology of Tallaght. Other saints of the house included Airennan, Eochaid, Joseph and Dichull. A bull of Alexander III joined Tallaght to the Archdiocese of Dublin in 1179. In 1223 its deanery passed to Saint Patrick's Cathedral. After the Reformation it fell to Protestant archbishops, and in 1812 the Dominicans bought its ruins and grounds, raising a novitiate and church there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-right:
Right, in this philosophical entry's sense, means a moral or lawful power over a thing: to hold it, claim it, and use it as one's own. When a person says he has a right to something, he claims a dominion over it that others must respect. Right is thus distinct from obligation: under an obligation we should act, while under a right we may act or refrain. It also differs from mere physical power: a thief may hold a stolen object without any right to it.

Every right answers to an obligation in others. If one person may demand a hundred dollars, another is bound to pay it, or the right would be empty. A thing here means not only material objects but anything useful to man, including actions and omissions. What counts as one's own is fixed by facts, from bodily faculties at birth to goods acquired later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gregory-of:
Gregory of Utrecht, abbot and disciple of Boniface, left a convent schoolroom to share the Apostle of Germany's hardships. Born about 707 or 708 to a noble Trier family, his father Alberic was son of Addula, widowed abbess of Pfalzel near Trier. A forged will and similar names long confused Addula with Adala, daughter of Dagobert II, falsely making Gregory Merovingian royalty. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 corrects the pedigree plainly.

Educated at Pfalzel, he read Scripture at meals when Boniface rested there in 722, travelling from Frisia toward Hessia and Thuringia. Boniface's warm account of apostolic life filled Gregory with enthusiasm, and nothing moved him from joining the mission. He became disciple, then helper, sharing Boniface's labours and journeys. The entry follows a boy reader who chose a missionary's road at a meal table.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-spanish-b:
Spain's corrida de toros, ill served by English bull-fight or German Stiergefecht, is the spectacle examined here. Origins divide opinion: some trace it to Rome's circus, where men faced wild beasts including bulls, while others, such as Nicolás de Moratín, look to ancient Celtiberian custom. Wild bulls infesting Spain first forced combat from necessity, then sport kept it alive.

Men who slew fierce beasts alone won heroic acclaim, as in the Calydonian boar tale, and brave men still sought glory once danger to life had passed. Ritual, matadors, picadors, and the Church's judgment follow, with moral debate running beside description. It is an entry that explains a national pastime without excusing or condemning it outright.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-dwight:
Thomas Dwight, an anatomist born at Boston in 1843, reshaped Harvard Medical School and won an international name in his field. He became a Catholic with his mother in 1856, graduated from Harvard Medical School in 1867, and in 1872 became instructor in comparative anatomy at Harvard. In 1883 he succeeded Oliver Wendell Holmes as Parkman professor of anatomy.

Dwight's gift for organization drove a needed rebuilding of the medical school, and his Warren Museum section on osteology was judged the best of its kind. His books included Frozen Sections of a Child in 1872 and a clinical atlas of hand and foot bones in 1907. His Thoughts of a Catholic Anatomist, published in 1911, argued that faith and science sit easily together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-utrecht:
Utrecht's archdiocese in the Netherlands covers Utrecht, Friesland, Overijssel, Drenthe, Groningen, most of Gelderland, and a small part of North Holland. In 1911 it counted 17 deaneries, 282 parishes, 578 secular priests, 390 churches and chapels, and 383,000 Catholics. Its cathedral chapter holds a provost and eight canons, and the government takes no part in naming the archbishop.

The seminary splits into two sections, one at Driebergen with five professors and one at Culemborg with twelve. Orders in the diocese include Augustinians, Carmelites, Capuchins, Dominicans, Franciscans, Trappists, and Redemptorists, with fifteen houses in all. The entry follows the see's history from its medieval bishops through the Reformation to its modern revival.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-peter-wri:
Peter Wright was a martyr born at Slipton in Northamptonshire in 1603, who suffered at Tyburn on 19 May 1651. Ten years in a country solicitor's office behind him, he joined the English army in Holland, deserted within a month, and passed two years at Ghent's Flemish Jesuit seminary. In 1629 he entered the Society's novitiate at Watten.

Various offices at Liège and Saint-Omer behind him, he turned chaplain to Sir Henry Gage's English regiment serving Spain. Gage's return to England in spring 1644 took Wright along, and he witnessed the relief of Basing House, home of John, fifth Marquess of Winchester. Present at Gage's death in January 1645, Wright became the marquess's chaplain in London, where he was arrested on Candlemas Day 1651 and condemned for his priesthood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-k:
William Knight was a Yorkshire layman executed at York in November 1596 for his Catholic faith. The son of Leonard Knight of South Duffield, he claimed property left by his father from a Protestant uncle, who denounced him to the authorities. He was seized at once and handed to a pursuivant, a priest-hunter, who treated him harshly.

Sent to York Castle in 1593, he joined fellow prisoners William Gibson and George Errington. A Protestant clergyman among them feigned a wish to convert, won their trust, and was directed to Henry Abbot, who tried to find him a priest. Abbot was then arrested, and all four were accused of persuading the clergyman to embrace Catholicism, treason under the penal laws. They were hanged, drawn, and quartered together, meeting death with joy and fortitude.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-wrigh:
William Wright was an English Jesuit scholar who defied the post-Gunpowder Plot oath of allegiance from prison. Born at York in 1562, he died on 18 January 1639. Coming late to study at twenty-three, he rose to teach philosophy for years at Gratz and Vienna. He joined the English mission after the Plot, served as chaplain at Hengrave Hall, and was arrested in July 1607, held in the Tower and the White Lion prison.

There Wright met his life's chance: Archpriest Blackwell had taken and praised the condemned loyalty oath, and Wright's brother Thomas backed it. But William disputed it with vigour and effect, and his Gage pupils refused it. When plague struck the prison, he nursed the sick, buried the dead, and escaped untouched in the confusion to Leicestershire missions. From 1612 he wrote some twelve volumes, three of controversy and the rest translations of Becan, Lessius, and others.
children-of-the-night:
Edwin Arlington Robinson published Children of the Night in 1897, his second book of poems, paid for in part by friends who believed in him when almost no one else did. Robinson wrote of his fictional Tilbury Town, a New England mill town of quiet failures, hidden griefs, and stubborn dignity. The poems are short, plain in speech, and deep in sympathy.

The book holds Richard Cory, his most famous poem, about the rich, envied man of the town who one calm summer night goes home and puts a bullet through his head. Luke Havergal, a cry of love and loss spoken at a western gate, is also here. President Theodore Roosevelt later read Robinson, praised him, and found him a clerk's post that let him keep writing.
city-of-endless-night:
City of Endless Night, by Milo Hastings, is a novel of a future Berlin sealed under a roof and ruled by a bred imperial line. The chapter heads alone map its world: synthetic beer, a narrator drafted for paternity, a eugenic staff, and a goddess suffering from obesity. Its narrator looks back on a childhood schooling steeped in German state texts.

Raised on a description of German life taken from a captured submarine, he grows into a visitor inside the endless city. Plot turns on revolt from within. A man named Zimmern confesses his hatred of the existing state and asks the narrator to stand with the rebels to the end. Their hope rests on flying men who bomb the roof of Berlin from the free world outside.
cobwebs-of-thought:
Cobwebs of Thought, by Arachne, is a set of philosophical essays that opens under a Voltaire epigraph on the soul. Essay I, Our Ignorance of Ourselves, attacks self-analysis head on. Probing the inner world of motive and desire, it argues, has seldom paid its practitioners.

Self-scrutiny without an aim outside the self breeds self-consciousness, and at times the beginnings of mental disease. Fruitful self knowledge needs a clear task, as in the psychology of Plato, Locke, Kant, and Descartes. A later essay turns to literature and takes up Hamlet. Against Maeterlinck, it argues that Hamlet was no fanatic for revenge: he spent his life weighing pros and cons, held to his task by love for his father.
critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-essay-8:
France in the eighteenth century, as told by M. Taine, is the subject of John Morley's eighth essay in his Critical Miscellanies, volume three. Macmillan published the volume in 1904. A contents list heads the essay, from Taine as a man of letters to a close on page 289.

Morley grants Taine's gifts but faults his method and his chief thesis. He says Taine rates letters too high as a cause of the social crisis. Court, nobles, and the state of France get their due weight instead. The lesson of the American Revolution enters near the end. Morley holds that the new ideas fared unlike in France and England because the ground they fell on differed. The essay is history reviewing history.
doe-osti-3006359-the-effect-of-luminance:
Pacific Northwest report for CRADA 653, dated September 2025, asks how the pattern of bright spots in an LED luminaire shapes discomfort glare at night. Six authors are listed, led by Belal Abboushi, Naomi Miller, and Michael Royer. In a dark laboratory, 29 participants viewed 68 stimuli that varied in spatial frequency, intensity, diffusion level, and ambient lighting. Each person rated discomfort from glare, whether individual LEDs could be resolved, and afterimages.

Higher spatial frequency raised both discomfort and the chance of afterimages. The authors suggest the eye's point spread function merges close sources into one larger, brighter-seeming source. Their practical advice favors luminaire designs with lower spatial frequencies. They also test the CIE-150:2017 intensity limits and find them too strict for some environmental zones, and they call for work tying ambient illuminance to each zone.
doe-osti-3012213-resistive-wall-simulati:
Resistive wall instability growth in the DARHT multi pulse test line is simulated by Carl Ekdahl of Los Alamos National Laboratory in LA-UR-25-32292. Several metres of the line may drift beam without external magnetic focusing, the worst case for the instability. Calculations used the LAMDA beam dynamics code, with a benchmark problem starting 1.0 millimetre off axis in a ten metre pipe.

For a pulse train, each successive pulse drifts a little further toward the wall than the one before. The final pulse carries the maximum displacement. That displacement stays substantially below what a single long pulse would show, and the pulse tail growth approaches exponential form over distance.
fighting-for-the-right:
Optic sends his hero back to war at sea in Fighting for the Right. Oliver Optic made the book one of his Blue and the Gray series, tales of the Civil War afloat. Its hero is Christy, a young Union officer. The series mates this sea set with a land set, Brother Against Brother and its kin.

The sampled pages put Christy in a harbor full of trade that fed the South. Cotton from Confederate ports crowds the wharves, landed by small craft that slipped the blockade. Christy had helped take a good number of such vessels. The visitors he sails with have no right to seize ships whose voyages are done, and the talk runs on the rules of capture. Optic mixes a boy's adventure with the real work of the blockade.
gunsight-pass-how-oil-came-to-the-cattle:
William MacLeod Raine published Gunsight Pass in 1921, with a subtitle that states its theme: how oil came to the cattle country and brought a new West. He dedicates it to James H. Langley, who lived many of these pages in his hot-blooded youth. The hero, Dave, is met first in a race and a quarrel; a chapter head calls a man crooked as a dog's hind leg. A paint horse disappears, and supper at Delmonico's is interrupted.

Then the tale darkens: a murder charge, and ten years. Dave comes back to a cattle land changed by oil, where old enemies and old friends wait. Raine, a Colorado man, knew both Wests, the cowman's and the oilman's. The book is a Western with a hinge in it, where the range gives way to the derrick.
he-knew-he-was-right:
Anthony Trollope's He Knew He Was Right was published in serial form in 1868 and 1869, as its transcriber's note records. Louis Trevelyan marries Emily Rowley and begins, the first chapter says, by shewing how wrath began. Colonel Osborne, a handsome family friend, visits too often for Trevelyan's peace. A quarrel progresses, is reconciled, and progresses again.

Trevelyan hires Bozzle, an ex-policeman, to watch his innocent wife. Miss Jemima Stanbury of Exeter shelters the Rowley sisters and supplies the comedy. Dorothy's suitors and Mr. Gibson's entanglements fill the Exeter chapters. Meanwhile jealousy hardens into monomania, and a jury's verdict of madness waits in the contents. Trollope's title is the tragedy's engine: a man who knew he was right, and was wrong, destroys his home to prove it. The novel stands among his darkest studies of marriage.
her-prairie-knight:
B M Bower published Her Prairie Knight under the name B M Sinclair, as this title page announces. Eastern heiress Beatrice Lansell is stranded on the prairie in chapter one when her party's wagon falters in a storm. A handsome cowboy, Keith Cameron, rides to the rescue, and her chaperone Mrs Lansell begins the lectures.

The English suitor Sir Redmond tilts with Keith while little Dorman plays Cupid and tears Beatrice's skirt chasing his fishes. The Pine Ridge range catches fire before Sir Redmond waits, and receives, his answer. Bower's early Western romance relies on her Montana knowledge: brands, weather, and cowboy talk carry the love story between an imperious girl and a foreman with a past.
is-ulster-right:
An anonymous Irishman argued Is Ulster Right? in London in 1913. The subtitle calls it a statement of the question between Ulster and the Nationalist Party. Historical, political, and financial reasons are promised for Ulster's stand against Home Rule. Chapters run from Celts and Danes through the Penal Laws to the Union.

Emmett's trial is recalled, with Plunket denouncing men who first fought Parliament, then rebelled for its loss. The Ulster Covenant and the bill before the country frame the argument. The danger to the Empire of Home Rule closes the case. It is a Unionist brief.
light:
Henri Barbusse wrote this novel, translated by Fitzwater Wray in 1919. Barbusse had already won fame as author of Under Fire. Twenty-three chapters run from Myself through Face to Face. Titles like The Storm, The Ruins, and Ghosts mark the route.

The narrator opens at his desk as the evening clock strikes seven. All his weekdays feel alike from beginning to end. Marie, brawlers, and apparitions disturb that dull routine. The closing chapters move toward the light of the title. Chapters named A Summary and The Brawler interrupt the quiet. De Profundis Clamavi and Eyes That See mark the spiritual turn.
literary-copyright:
Charles Dudley Warner addresses literary copyright in this piece. The text opens at the National Institute of Arts and Letters. That body held its first public meeting under discussion here. Members came by invitation from the American Social Science Association.

At Saratoga Springs in September 1899, members voted for independence. They adopted a revised constitution agreed upon in New York. The institute's object is advancing art and literature, Warner explains. Membership requires notable achievement in art or letters. Active membership would probably settle near one hundred, Warner reports. Honorary and associate members could join without numerical limit.
love-at-second-sight:
Love at Second Sight is a society novel by Ada Leverson, first published in 1916. It is book three of her Little Ottleys series. The story opens with a crash, shrieks, and a quarrel on a staircase. Edith Ottley rises from her blue sofa to find her son Archie blaming Madame Frabelle.

Archie is a calm boy of ten with sly humor in his glance. Around Edith's home moves the world of London drawing rooms. Visits, guests, and love affairs fill Leverson's light, witty pages. She writes of marriage and manners with a gentle sting. The novel charms readers who like quiet comedy of society.
midnight:
Octavus Roy Cohen published this detective novel in 1921. Cohen was already known for The Crimson Alibi and Gray Dusk. The story begins out of a storm, with a suit-case that must be opened. A chapter heading gives the detective's rule: find the woman.

The investigator Carroll interviews visitors, a valet, and several women tied to the case. Hazel Gresham, Evelyn Rogers, and Roland Warren all enter the inquiry. Later chapters return to the suit-case, a woman in a taxi, and a suspect with no alibi. Cohen builds a period mystery of clues, accusations, and loose ends.
nasa-tm-19650003087-pressure-measurement:
Earl R Keener, at the High-Speed Flight Station at Edwards in California, reported flight pressure readings for a delta wing in October 1959. The wing was conically cambered, meaning its surface was curved in a cone-like way. The aircraft was the F-102A, and speeds were transonic, near the speed of sound.

Keener presents pressures measured in real flight, not in a tunnel. Flight data check whether tunnel results hold on a real aircraft. For a cambered delta wing, those readings matter for lift and control. The report preserves that measured record.
nasa-tm-19670026211-preliminary-results-:
C. Catoe, W. Nordberg, P. Thaddeus, and G. Ling, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this report in August 1967. It gives early results from aircraft flight tests of an electrically scanning microwave radiometer. The instrument was designed for a meteorological satellite, and scanning its beam electronically, with no moving antenna, promised a sturdier sensor.

Flown on NASA's Convair 990 aircraft, the radiometer proved that satellite radiation measurements could extend from the infrared into much longer microwave wavelengths. Its phased-array antenna swept a narrow beam sideways across the flight path, building two-dimensional maps of Earth's brightness temperature. Flights crossed Arctic Ocean ice, Alaskan tundra and snow, southwestern deserts, midwestern farmland, Yucatan forests, and storms over land and water. Preliminary displays showed the instrument performing as expected. Land-water and ice contrasts mapped clearly under all cloud conditions, and ocean storm activity could be identified positively.
nasa-tm-19670028348-synthesis-of-ultrahi:
Li-Chen Hsu, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, presented this paper at a polymers meeting in Cleveland, Ohio, in April 1967. It covers the making of poly(ethylene terephthalate), the plastic called PET, with very long molecule chains. Such ultrahigh molecular weight material was wanted to test how chain length affects PET's behavior at cryogenic temperatures, where aerospace uses were in view.

Hsu prepared PET with an average molecular weight on the order of one hundred twenty thousand, starting from commercial grade material. The reaction ran in the solid state inside a gas chromatograph apparatus, an unusual piece of equipment for polymer synthesis. Parameters studied included the catalyst, particle size, and the molecular weight of the starting material. Reaction temperature and time mattered, as did the nature and flow rate of the carrier gas sweeping through the apparatus.
nasa-tm-19690018398-sounding-rocket-para:
Brian C. Pierman, of Goddard Space Flight Center's Flight Program Office, prepared this March 1969 report, X-326-69-162, on sounding rocket parameters versus flight reliability. He compares two physical parameters, flight weight and telemetry channel count, against flight failure rates. The purpose is practical: choosing which environmental tests sounding rocket payloads should have to pass before flying.

A clear correlation is established between greater weight and decreased flight success, Pierman reports. No correlation is established between telemetry channels and flight success. Charts track failure percentages for Apache and Aerobee rockets across moving weight brackets. The finding gives test planners a simple rule: heavier payloads deserve the closer look, while channel count alone signals nothing.
now-or-never-or-the-adventures-of-bobby-:
Oliver Optic wrote Now or Never, or the Adventures of Bobby Bright, as a story for young folks. William T. Adams, his real name, entered it in Massachusetts in 1856. This new edition came from the Mershon Company in New York, under an 1884 copyright. The book is dedicated to his nephew, Charles Henry Pope.

A front picture shows Bobby declaring he is big enough to protect his mother, and will do it. That line, from page forty-two, sets the hero's stamp. Optic wrote boys who work, save, and stand up at home. Young America of his day read such tales for both fun and example. Bobby's adventures test a poor boy's grit.
pictures-in-colour-of-the-isle-of-wight:
Pictures in Colour of the Isle of Wight, from Jarrold and Sons, contains fifty coloured pictures with descriptive notes. The foreword calls the island a resort of varied attractions: cliffs and bays for coast scenery, old mills and cottages for lovers of sylvan beauty. The rugged Landslip and Undercliff furnish romantic interest. Geologists, it adds, can study many formations within short distances, and botanists find wild flowers and ferns in variety.

The pictures reproduce actual photographs, true to nature. The first note treats Steephill Castle near Ventnor. The book ends by calling the island the Garden of England, and inviting readers to come and see.
raabe-german-moonlight:
Moonlight falls on small-town Germany in Wilhelm Raabe's novella German Moonlight, presented here in English. Ordinary people carry inner lives far richer than their quiet streets suggest. Raabe, often called the German Dickens, specialized in exactly that discovery, and this tale shows his method at its gentlest.

Warm humor and quiet melancholy share the telling, as old memories stir under the moon's calm light. Nothing sensational happens; everything human does. Raabe trusted readers to find depth without being shouted at. The novella makes a gentle, moonlit entry into his large and rewarding body of work. Those who enjoy it will find a whole shelf of his fiction waiting in both languages.
recent-developments-in-european-thought:
F. S. Marvin arranged and edited this set of essays on fresh turns in European thought, issued by Oxford University Press in 1920. The book belongs to the Unity Series, and Marvin, author of The Living Past, wrote its opening general survey himself. A line from Shelley's Prometheus Unbound stands as the book's motto.

Four scholars then take up one field each. Professor A. E. Taylor of St. Andrews writes on philosophy, and Dr. F. B. Jevons of Durham on religion. Professor C. H. Herford of Manchester treats poetry, and G. P. Gooch treats history. Each essay maps what had lately changed in its field for general readers.
ships-that-pass-in-the-night:
A two-part novel unfolds in these chapters, with no author named on the pages at hand. Part One brings a newcomer to a health resort world, where Mrs. Reffold learns her lesson and a figure called the Disagreeable Man draws all eyes. Bernardine stands at the tale's warm center.

Chapters trace a betrothal, a love letter, and ships that speak each other in passing. Part Two opens with the dusting of books. Invalids, travelers, and caretakers cross paths briefly and part changed. The title's image of brief meetings governs a tale of kindness between strangers who may never meet again.
swimming-scientifically-taught:
Prof. Frank Eugen Dalton, instructor in scientific swimming at the Dalton Swimming School and originator of the Dalton Method, wrote Swimming Scientifically Taught as a practical manual for young and old. A portrait of Dalton fronts the title page, and a chapter on advanced strokes by Louis C. Dalton of the same school completes the book.

The Daltons teach swimming as a science of strokes, breathing, and body position rather than a knack picked up by splashing. Their method aimed at learners who feared the water as much as at swimmers chasing form and speed. Manuals of this kind, sold with a named system and a family school behind it, belonged to the age when physical culture experts promised methodical mastery of every bodily art.
the-boy-knight: G. A. Henty wrote The Boy Knight: A Tale of the Crusades, dated 1882. Henty had also written The Young Buglers, Through the Fray, The Cornet of Horse, and The Young Colonists. The chapter list starts with The Outlaws and A Rescue. The Capture of Wortham Hold comes third. Then a chapter named for the Crusades leads into making ready, the lists, revenge, and the attack. The list stops at the ninth chapter, whose head is not shown. No page of the tale itself is given here.
the-celtic-twilight:
W. B. Yeats opens this Irish book with a short poem on time and decay, then a verse piece called The Hosting of the Sidhe. In that poem the fairy host rides from Knocknarea, with Caolte tossing his burning hair and Niamh calling mortals away. The host warns that it comes between any watcher and both the deed of his hand and the hope of his heart.

A prose opening, headed This Book, states Yeats's method plainly. He wished, like every artist, to build a small world from the fine and telling things of a flawed world. He aimed to show something of the face of Ireland to his own people. So he wrote down, with care and candor, much that he had heard and seen, adding little that he had merely made up.
the-child-under-eight: E. R. Murray, Vice-Principal of Maria Grey Training College, and Henrietta Brown Smith, a lecturer at Goldsmiths' College, wrote this study of young children in the Modern Educator's Library, dated 1920. Only the series list, title page, and a motto from Thomas Traherne are present here. The motto marvels that an infant is heir of the whole world.Beyond the front matter, nothing is present to describe.
the-chums-of-scranton-high-or-hugh-morga: Donald Ferguson wrote this boys' school story, copyrighted in 1919 by the Goldsmith Publishing Company of Cleveland. Only the title page and contents are present here, with a frontispiece line in which Hugh speaks sternly. The chapters follow Hugh Morgan through a heavy task, a tragic affair on the road, a trap, a rescue at Hobson's Mill-Pond, and a straight drive for the truth.The chapters themselves remain out of view.
the-city-of-dreadful-night:
James Thomson's long poem opens under two dark mottoes, one from Dante and one from Leopardi. Dante's line points to the city of pain, and the Leopardi passage holds that fate denies blessedness to both the living and the dead. A proem in verse then explains why such a poem gets written at all.

The speaker writes, he says, prostrate in the dust, out of his heart's deep languor and his soul's sad tears. He asks why he should dig up dead faith and break the seals of mute despair. His answer is a cold rage that seizes him at times, driving him to show the bitter, wrinkled truth stripped of false dreams, false hopes, and the masks of youth. Fashioning woe into living words, however rough, gives some sense of power and passion. He writes not for the hopeful young, he warns, but for those who share his night.
the-fiend-s-delight:
Dod Grile, a pen name, gathered short comic tales in The Fiend's Delight, printed at New York in 1873. A mock preface and a sly dedication to the goddess Good Taste open the book.

The contents list dozens of brief sketches: One More Unfortunate, The Strong Young Man of Colusa, A Tale of the Great Quake, and Mr. Grile's Girl among them. West coast life, mining camps, and small town frauds feed the jokes. The tone is dry and cutting, in the school of tall tales told dead-pan, where fools, rogues, and bores each get a short, sharp lesson.
the-gibson-upright: Booth Tarkington and Harry Leon Wilson wrote The Gibson Upright as a play, printed in 1919. Only the front matter is present here. The cast list names Andrew Gibson, a piano factory owner. It names Nora Gorodna, a piano tester and socialist labor organizer. A socialist journalist stands in the list. A crew of factory workers, old and young, stands with them. Wives and a truck driver fill out the cast. A note says Stuart Walker staged the play. No scene or speech can be read here.
the-ignatian-epistles-entirely-spurious-:
W. D. Killen wrote this reply to Bishop Lightfoot of Durham. Killen taught church history in Ireland. He led the Presbyterian theological faculty there. Edinburgh saw the book in 1886. Lightfoot had argued for the letters of Ignatius. Seven letters are ascribed to that early martyr. Lightfoot called them genuine. He ranked them among the best proved writings of old times.

Killen's title gives the opposite verdict. The letters are wholly spurious, he argues. His preface protests against easy trust in a famous name. Such trust will sway a wide circle of readers. It would also upset the sound rules of history. He quotes Neander on the letters' weak stamp of a real man's voice. He praises Lightfoot's work on Scripture itself. The errors of a famed writer, he says, most need a challenge.
the-ladies-delight:
Printed for W. James in the Strand in 1732, this bawdy pamphlet cost sixpence. It gathers an address to all well provided Hibernians. A poem called The Arbor Vitae or Tree of Life follows. A prose natural history of the same tree comes next. A poem on Ridotto al' Fresco closes it. That poem describes the tree's growth in the Spring Gardens at Vauxhall. An ingenious botanist tends it there. The Latin motto warns that pleasure is a serious business.

The address opens the joke in a sustained plant metaphor. Irish gentlemen are congratulated on their gardens' largest trees. The ladies caress them for those trees, it says. Men of less parts are laughed at and shut out of company. The satire is a period piece of Grub-Street erotica. Innuendo about fruit, branches, and hopeful sticks fills it. A knowing coffee-house readership was its aim.
the-long-night: Stanley Weyman's The Long Night was issued by Longmans, Green, and Company in 1903, marked as a second impression. Only the title page, a list of Weyman's works, and part of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapters open with A Student of Theology and The House on the Ramparts. Then come The Quintessential Stone, Caesar Basterga, The Elixir Vitae, and Melusina, pointing to a tale with alchemy in it. Weyman's listed works include A Gentleman of France and Under the Red Robe.
the-man-in-the-twilight: Ridgwell Cullum's The Man in the Twilight was published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1922. Only the title pages, a list of Cullum's novels, a dedication to his nephew, and an author's note are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. In that note Cullum stresses that his story of the Sachigo wood-pulp mills is a work of imagination. He drew heavily on his knowledge of the wood-pulp trade of Eastern Canada. The book contains no portrait of any person and no real business organisation.
the-northern-light:
E. Werner wrote the German novel The Northern Light, and Mrs. D. M. Lowrey translated it into English for this 1891 edition. Werner had earlier written At a High Price and His Word of Honor. The story opens on a grey autumn morning at a large manor house by a forest.

Two men watch birds fly south for the winter and talk about their own lives. One is a tall, blond officer named Falkenried, still young but already worn by care. His older companion tells him he takes life too hard. Their talk sets a somber mood of age, duty, and lost youth for the tale that follows.
the-princess-priscilla-s-fortnight:
Her Grand Ducal Highness the Princess Priscilla of Lothen-Kunitz was, up to twenty-one, a most promising young lady. She did what she was told, or better, sensed what was wanted and did it unasked. Her father, once fiery, is now an irritable old gentleman who insists on strict etiquette and is proud of her when she crosses his mind. Her English mother, original to the end, died when Priscilla was sixteen. Her two plainer sisters each married a suitable prince.

Priscilla herself is tall, with a long pointed chin and a sweet, kind mouth. Her nose is not quite straight, a slight crookedness the narrator finds charming beyond chiselled features. The book appeared in 1905 as by the author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden; an editorial note names that author as Elizabeth von Arnim. The narrator promises to describe Priscilla's dreadful conduct.
the-secret-of-the-night: Gaston Leroux's The Secret of the Night is dated 1912 in its header. The pages shown give a contents list of eighteen chapters and no story text. The first chapter is Gayety and Dynamite. Natacha, the watch, and a mysterious hand follow. Living bombs and marshes come later. A revolutionary tribunal and the last cravat close the list. A sibling record of this novel prints one chapter more, The Tsar.
the-street-called-straight:
Basil King published this novel in May 1912. He also wrote The Inner Shrine. Grosset and Dunlap issued it by arrangement with Harper and Brothers. Orson Lowell illustrated it. A New England motto heads the book. It speaks of coming by the street called Straight to the house called Beautiful. Chapter one finds Davenant back in the company of the hostess who once refused him.

Davenant is under no illusions about his welcome, King writes, but takes a mild pleasure in curiosity, admiration, and reminiscent suffering whose sting time has drawn. Between twenty-four and thirty-three, work and travel taught him much. A wider knowledge of men helped too. He now sees his proposal to Miss Guion as she saw it then. It was so ill-matched and absurd that it called for no reply. Not even a short no was needed.
the-tavern-knight: Rafael Sabatini's Tavern Knight, his 1904 novel, is represented here by a title and chapter list alone, with no page of the story itself. Eighteen chapters are named, opening on the march, passing through Worcester Field, and reaching the tavern knight's own story at chapter seven. Later headings promise an escape, the Ashburns, a metamorphosis of Kenneth, a reckoning, and a counter-plot. The skeleton points to an English Civil War adventure of loyalty and disguise, but Sabatini's swashbuckling prose remains outside this record.
thirty-years-in-hell-or-from-darkness-to: Ex-priest Bernard Fresenborg announced Thirty Years in Hell, or, From Darkness to Light, published at St. Louis and entered for copyright in 1904. Its title page says he spent thirty years in Roman Catholicism and now denounces it. The book runs to about four hundred large pages. Promotional lines call every page a stinging rebuke to Catholicism, and an author's announcement begins after the title matter. What is present here is the announcement's opening and the title pages, so Fresenborg's chapters themselves do not appear.
twelfth-night: Only production notes open this record, signed by Michael S. Hart of Project Gutenberg. The notes explain why the spelling in these old Shakespeare texts looks wrong to modern eyes. Printers, Hart says, packed type into blocks and swapped letters such as u and v when sorts ran short. He quotes three lines of Hamlet to show the old spellings kept unchanged here. No scene of the play itself is present in these pages.
waysiders-stories-of-connacht:
Seumas O'Kelly, author of The Shuiler's Child and The Lady of Deerpark, wrote Waysiders, stories of Connacht, issued at New York in 1918. The contents name ten tales. The Can with the Diamond Notch, Both Sides of the Pond, and The White Goat lead. The Sick Call, The Shoemaker, The Rector, and The Home-Coming follow. A Wayside Burial, The Gray Lake, and The Building close the list. The first tale opens on a shop sign in the west of Ireland.

The name stands out in chaste white letters on a black board. The shop itself seems to spring from the landscape with an air of aggression. It proclaims, he says, the clash of two civilisations, with the hills pitched against it. From such small fronts O'Kelly builds the inner life of Connacht villages, where old ways meet new money.
